speechtext: Bill No. 210, for the relief of Frederick Dwight Ghesley.-Mr. Baker.
On the Orders of the Day being called:

I desire to ask the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Roche) what the position is with regard to the Hindu immigrants, who, I understand, arrived at Vancouver some days ago. I am told by the Prime Minister that the law will be enforced. What I am anxious to know is, will the clause of the immigration law which takes into the control of the Government, to the exclusion of the courts, the right to deal with immigrants, be acted upon?
Mr. ROGHiE: I have been out of the city for a couple of days. I asked this morning if anything new 'had arisen in connection with the Hindus, who, I believe, are about a mile outside the port of Vancouver and are undergoing a thorough examination by the officials of the department. The Order in Council passed some time ago prohibiting the immigration of labourers will, of course, be called into requisition .in this case, .and absolutely

acted upon and enforced. That is what the hon. gentleman refers to, is it not?

No, I am referring to the provision of the Act which was ignored in the case of the sixteen Hindus which were admitted .some weeks or months ago-the provision which sets aside the authority of the courts until the immigrants have been passed by the officials of the Department of the Interior and have been officially Landed. Is the Government going to stand on that section of the Act?

The Government are first going to utilize this Order in Council. Failing that, of course, as to those whom we cannot prohibit by that Order in Council, we will call into use the regulations amended in accordance with the decision of Chief Justice Hunter. There were defects in the old Order in 'Council. This has been remedied, and I think it will hold water even against the decision of the Chief Justice. We are going to stand by the immigration law in its fullness.
On the Orders of the Day being called:

I am asked by a correspondent who seems to be well informed to call the attention of the Minister of the Interior to the fact that a .large number of Hungarians and Russians have landed lately in Quebec, and instead of taking up farm work remain in the city; also that a large number of assisted immigrants are being sent to Canada by the Unemployment Committee of London, England, Is the Minister of the Interior aware of that fact?

I am not aware of any association who :a.re bringing labourers to Canada at all. I am certain that all officials under the jurisdiction of the department, and steamship agencies a3 well, have been notified to adhere rigidly to the instructions that no immigrants coming to Canada should be encouraged except those of the agricultural class.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to ask you or whoever has the power to answer, under what authority the Library

and the reading room were closed from early Sunday evening until this morning- closed all day yesterday. There are a great many holidays; we had one last week, we have had one this week, and shall probably have one next week. While these holidays are no inconvenience-probably the reverse, a decided advantage- to the members who live near Ottawa, to nearly all the members from Ontario and Quebec they are a great disadvantage to the members from the far East or West who are obliged to spend the whole session in Ottawa. On the holidays we have hitherto been allowed the privilege of the reading room and Library, but on this occasion even that was taken away from us. That seems to me a strange thing, and I ask under what authority it was done.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: CLOSING OF LIBRARY AND READING ROOM ON HOLIDAYS.
speechtext:
As the hon. gentleman
knows, a joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons is concerned with matters relating to the Library. I am not aware what the practice is in regard to closing the Library during the session of Parliament, but I do not suppose that any departure from the usual custom has been made. My recollection is that on public holidays the Library is always closed.

maintopic: CLOSING OF LIBRARY AND READING ROOM ON HOLIDAYS.
speechtext:
The reading room was
closed as well.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: CLOSING OF LIBRARY AND READING ROOM ON HOLIDAYS.
speechtext: Is that a departure from what has taken place in the past?

maintopic: CLOSING OF LIBRARY AND READING ROOM ON HOLIDAYS.
speechtext:
So far as I recollect, it
is.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: CLOSING OF LIBRARY AND READING ROOM ON HOLIDAYS.
speechtext: The Librarian drew my attention to the fact that yesterday was a public holiday and said that the custom was for the Library to close during public holidays, and requested me to consent to its being closed. He also mentioned that as this holiday immediately followed Sunday the great majority of the members had gone home and he did not think there would be anybody resorting to the Library, and asked permission to close it on Sunday. I said, if it was the custom, to carry out the custom. I had a request also with regard to the reading room, and was told that the custom was to 'dose it when the Library was closed. I gave instructions that the reading room was to be kept open from ten to four. I do not know by what misunderstanding it was closed.

Consideration in Committee of resolutions respecting the Canadian Northern railway, resumed from Wednesday, May 20, Mr. Biondin in the Chair.
1. That His Majesty on behalf of the Dominion of Canada may aid the construction, completion, equipment and betterment of the Canadian Northern system by guaranteeing payment of the principal and interest of the bonds, debentures, debenture stock and other securities, hereinafter called the guaranteed securities of the Canadian Northern, to an amount not exceeding forty-five million dollars ($45,000,000) which guaranteed securities, to the extent aforesaid, the Canadian Northern is hereby authorized to create and issue; interest on the guaranteed securities to be at the rate of four per cent per annum payable half-yearly, the principal to be payable not later than a day in the year 1934.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend is speaking of what mortgage now?

The mortgage to the
British Empire Trust Company?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Of what date?

November 19, 1913. My right hon. friend will remember that the onily security which the Government ha= is in the equity of redemption in the stock of the Canadian Northern Town Properties Company, which is mentioned in this mortgage to the British Empire Trust Company. The matter is rather complicated, but that is the result of it. As to the Solicitor General's statement with regard to the inclusion of British Columbia townsites. I have had very little opportunity of studying the mortgage, but I cannot find a single townsite in British Columbia mentioned with the exception of Port Mann. If that is so, my hon. friend, I am sure, will feel that he ought to correct the error into which he led the House and the country, because he made that statement very positively and sought to lead the committee to believe that there were very valuable securities in connection with townsites in British Columbia.
Mr. ME1GHEN: Would the hon. gentleman explain the power to release a little more fully?
That is contained in the 15th section, paragraph c.
That gives the Townsites Properties, Limited, power to release certain lands.

No, it gives the Canadian Northern or Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, power. ' The company ' means the Canadian Northern Railway Company. Section 15, paragraph c, is as follows:
(c) The company (which means the Canadian Northern Railway Company) shall have the right to sell or contract for the sale of the whole or any part of the mortgaged lands at any price not being less than such a sum as will together with the purchase price of all lands forming part of the mortgaged lands sold or contracted to be sold by the company subsequent to the 30th October, 1913, be equal to an average of $15 per acre for all the mortgaged lands so sold or contracted to be sold, inclusive of the land in respect of which such sum is to be paid and pending the carrying out of the provisions of clause 10 hereof, the company or Mackenzie and Mann and Company-
That is the Canadian Northern Railway Company or Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited.
-shall have the like right to sell or contract for the sale of the whole or any part of the properties and premises mentioned in the third schedule hereto (hereinafter referred to as the 'town properties') at any price not being less than such sum as will together with the purchase price of all town properties sold or contracted to be sold subsequent to the 30th October, 1913, be equal to an average of $150 per acre for all the town properties so sold or contracted to be sold inclusive of the town property in respect of which such sum is to be paid. The company and Mackenzie, Mann and Company as the case may require shall be entitled to convey or to have conveyed any part of the mortgaged lands and town properties so sold or contracted to be sold by it as aforesaid to the purchaser freed and discharged from the trusts of these presents upon payment to the trustees (or to the trustees for the bonds of 1899 or the bonds of 1909 or the Government of Canada where such trustees or Government have a prior right thereto) of the net purchase money therefor remaining after payment thereout of all such costs, charges and expenses as mentioned in clause 16 hereof and the trustees shall be bound to execute and do all assurances, deeds, documents and things which may be necessary for that purpose. And any of the mortgaged lands and town properties may be sold wholly or partly on credit but provided that the purchaser shall not be entitled to receive a conveyance until the net purchase money has been paid in full but any such purchaser may receive from the company a contract in evidence of his purchase. Provided always that the trustees may in their discretion allow and if necessary concur in executing a conveyance to the purchaser and accept from the purchaser a mortgagee or other security and covenant or other obligation
for the payment of the purchase money and interest (if any) or any unpaid part thereof.
(d) The trustees shall not be concerned or entitled to inquire whether the person put forward by the company of Mackenzie, Mann and Company to receive a conveyance of any part of the mortgaged lands or town properties is or is not the purchaser or otherwise the proper person to receive such conveyance and the trustees shall not be liable for having at the request of the company or Mackenzie, Mann and Company conveyed or consented to the conveyance to any person nothwithstanding that it shall at any time thereafter appear that such person was not the purchaser or otherwise the proper person to receive such conveyance.	.
My reading of that is that the company or Mackenzie, Mann and Company, that is, the Canadian Northern Railway Company, or the Mackenzie-Mann Company, Limited, shall, notwithstanding this trust mortgage, have the right to withdraw any of the farm lands on paying in $15 per acre upon the lands so to be withdrawn, or any of the lands in the townsites on paying in $150 per acre and requiring the trustees, on the receipt of that sum, less any expenses, to execute conveyances to the people to whom the Canadian Northern railway or Mackenzie, Mann and Company, have sold any of the lands. If that is so, my hon. friend, I think, will agree with me that the security which the Government have taken upon the equity of redemption in this stock of the Canadian Northerm Town Properties Company will' be of very little value and that this provision will be likely to induce the Canadian Northern railway or Mackenzie, Mann and Company to execute some conveyances which will release that privilege which they have of withdrawing lands. Take Port Mann. Supposing there are six hundred acres in that townsite. The whole property could be withdrawn under sale by Mackenzie, Mann and Company, or the Canadian Northern Railway Company, to any purchaser on payment to the trustees of $9,000; whereas the townsite, as we all know, is to-day, or was at one time, worth a great many hundreds of thousands of dollars, probably up into the millions.

On the first question raised by the hon. gentleman, when the point came up last Tuesday or Wednesday whether Port Mann was included in the properties belonging to the Canadian Northern Town Properties, Limited, I did not profess to be familiar with every item covered in these eight or nine pages. Consequently I deferred explaining whether it was in or not. In the meantime, however, the hon. member for St. John (Mr. COMMONS
Pugsley) informed the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Neely) that the townsite of Port Mann was not in.
I was looking at the fourth schedule.

So that the first explanation to the House for any error that may have been committed is due from the hon. member for St. John, as the townsite of Port Mann clearly is included. In the course of my explanation, if I remember my remarks correctly, I did state that the other townsites in British Columbia were included. That I believed to be correct, and I still believe that to be correct. The hon. member for St. John must remember that Town Properties, Limited, have been in existence for some time, and any townsites that have been handled since it was formed have been handled solely as the property of Town Properties, Limited. I think I am correct in saying that any other townsites in British Columbia are included. I thought at the time that Coquitlam was in previous to the incorporation, but perhaps it was not. At all events, the effect is the same; if they have been taken by Town Properties, Limited, since incorporation, they consequently will not be included in the schedule, but they will be in the security just the same.
As to the other point, the hon. gentleman seemed to think that there is a clause in this trust deed which will weaken or detract from the value of the stock and bonds of Town Properties, Limited, in that it provides for the extraction of certain lands in acreage amounts from the mortgage on payment of so much. I do not profess to be familiar with the exact details of all these clauses, but in so far as my knowledge of such things goes, I would think the reason for this provision would be that Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, and the Canadian Northern railway, found it necessary, in view of lands having been sold by them, to provide that certain acreages might be taken out from the mortgage in order that they might complete their titles. That is the way it would appear to me, that is the purpose of the clause, and they fixed the price in such a way that they would be safe in taking the land at that figure. Fifteen dollars per acre would be about the price for farm lands. The hon. member will find in the documents laid on the table that that is the average price of farm lands in the statement in which they make up a total of some $29,150,000 as the value accruing to the Canadian Northern Railway Company

from farm lands that could have been retained by Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, as their individual property.
I do not know at the present time why $150 an acre has been fixed for general property, but I scarcely think that price would apply to Port Mann or any other property that can be taken by the Canadian Northern Railway Company. Whatever property isi taken by the Canadian Northern Railway Company is then owned by the Canadian Northern, and if there is any advantage in it the Canadian Northern gets that advantage, and as the assets of the Canadian Northern are mortgaged by the trust deed the Government also gets- that advantage. I venture to say, although I do [DOT]not pretend to have a detailed knowledge of this just now, that there is no provision by which advantage will accrue to Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, as against Townsite Properties, Limited. The stocks and bonds of Town Properties-, Limited, represent its assets and they are held by Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, subject to the pledge given under the trust deed. Consequently, we would get the equity in their stocks and bonds, we would get all that Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, have in Town Properties, Limited, -and that is all we set out to get,

My hon. friend seems to be very reluctant to be convinced that he is wrong. I cannot see that there is a possibility of his being right in his suggestion that Port Mann would not be included in the provisions of paragraph c. Paragraph c is expressly made applicable to all the town properties mentioned in the third schedule, and it is in the third schedule that Port Mann is included (as will be seen on page 43), and it is the only town-site in British Columbia mentioned,
We will see about that.

When my hon. friend
who has -charge of this agreement, and who has had weeks and weeks to inform himself with regard to its provisions and with regard to the security which is being taken by the Government, and whose word is intended to go to the country with a view to inducing the people to believe that this Government has taken all the security it possibly can- when my hon. friend makes the erroneous statement that there are a number of valuable townsites in British Columbia in addition to Port Mann-

Does my hon. friend
question my statement that he said several townsites in British Columbia were included?
You just added the word ' valuable ' without authority-that is all.

It was my hon. friend from Humboldt who used the word ' valuable.' I noticed in the Government press, in fact in all the papers both Government and Opposition, that my hon. friend had stated that there were a number of town-sites in British Columbia which were included besides Port Mann, and the hon. member for Humboldt admitted that these would be very valuable. At all events, it is the fact, so far as the papers before the House are concerned, and upon which the House is asked to vote, that the townsites in British Columbia are not included unless perhaps the townsite of Port Mann. My hon. friend says that everything belonging to the Canadian Northern passes over to the Government. My hon. friend may be right, but I do not so understand it. I understand there are a number of very valuable properties which do not pass; for instance, the railway interests in Nova Scotia, known as the Inverness Railway and Coal Company.
That does not belong to the Canadian Northern.
I venture to say it does.
I venture to say it does not.
Or to Mackenzie and Mann.
Oh, oh! I thought we should see from whom the apology was due.
My hon. friend says it belongs to Mackenzie and Mann.
I did not say that at all.

If my hon. friend had looked into the matter more carefully, he would have seen that it is of importance to the country that all the various properties owned by Mackenzie and Mann should go in as security.

While on this point, will the hon. gentleman tell the House what is
the annual income of the Inverness Company, whether or not there has been an annual deficit, and what are the grounds for his assertion that, that railway would be a valuable asset?

I am not sufficiently
familiar with it to tell my hon. friend.
Had not the hon. gentleman better get familiar with it before he talks about -it being a valuable asset?

Does my hon. friend
say it would not be a valuable asset?
I do.

My hon. friend who represents that section of Nova Scotia thinks it ought to 'be included. I venture to say that it is just as valuable an asset and earns just as much as the Halifax and Southwestern railway.

I am surprised to hear the Solicitor General say that this road is not going to be a valuable asset. The hon. gentleman must remember that this line is serving a very important coal mine at Inverness and is also about to serve an important coal mine at Mabou. It is also destined to serve another coal mine at Port Hood, -which is temporarily closed down but will eventually be opened up. More than that, my hon. friend must remember that Mackenzie and Mann are now endeavouring to secure a very valuable property ten miles north of the present terminus of the Inverness Railway Company When Mackenzie and Mann have secured that property and extended the road to it, they will be carrying the products of four coal mines, and I am surprised to hear the Solicitor General say that this road is not destined to be -a very valuable railway. Not only that-but I believe that if Mackenzie and Mann secure -the coal property at St. Rose and Chimney Comer they will extend their road to these collieries, and in order to carry out their obligations to the county of Inverness they must construct the road to Chetieamp. One reason why -they are not extending the road, as was the intent of their agreement with the municipality of Inverness, is that they first want to get hold of the coal property at St. Rose and Chimney Corner aforesaid, situated ten miles north of their present terminus. That is my own opinion. They want this property, and being selfish they are acting the dog in the manger; they will not extend the road because that might enable the present owners of the coal property to demand a -better price for their property.

Mackenzie and Mann want to get possession of this coal mine at their own price. Going a little further, this country north of Inverness has a very great quantity of valuable minerals in the form of gypsum, copper and pyrites; the road will also go through one of the finest farming sections in Nova Scotia. A most valuable fishing industry will also be developed. If the Solicitor General will take the trouble to look into the natural assets of North Inverness, he will have no hesitation in determining that this road is destined to be one of the best paying roads in Nova Scotia. I would remind him too tliat the net earning power of the road last year was a little over $80,000.
Does the hon. gentleman mean over operating expenses?
Over operating expenses.

But not including the
bond issue?

I am not talking about the bond issue. There is a history to that into which I will not go just now. It would be well for this Government to inquire into this situation and see that this road is included in the schedule. I cannot see why Mackenzie and Mann should be opposed to it. I see every reason why the Government should come to the rescue of the people of Inverness. One reason is that by including this road in the schedule the people of Inverness will have some tribunal to which they can appeal for redress of their grievances. They have many grievances in respect to freight rates, and other matters which I cannot enumerate just now. If the placing of the Mackenzie and Mann possessions in Inverness in these schedules would bring the road under the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission it would be a great relief to the people of that county. If I were supporting a Government that would not take advantage of the present opportunity to compel Mackenzie and Mann to carry out their agreement with the county of Inverness I would withdraw my support from them, without the slightest hesitation. It is a deplorable thing that a great corporation like Mackenzie, Mann and Company, should enter into an agreement with the municipality of Inverness and should be allowed to carry out only that part of the agreement that brings the road to their own property and stops there, and get the municipal subventions for and refuse to fulfil their part of the bargain. They got the money

of the people of Inverness; they got a bonus of $1,000 a mile and a free right of way under false pretences. Mackenzie, Mann and Company took these moneys from the people of Inverness for the construction of this road to their private property at Inverness, and they are doing nothing in the world to carry out their agreement with respect to the extension of the road North to Cheticamp. It may be said that the municipality of Inverness have a recourse against them, that they should go to the courts. Well, the people of Inverness are not disposed to go into the courts on a question of this kind, with a corporation that has treated them as this company did. They are fearful of lawyers and of courts and I- do not blame them. I would invite hon. gentlemen opposite to look into that agreement between Mackenzie and Mann and the municipality of Inverness, and I believe that they will see that Mackenzie and Mann are compelled to do one of two things: either carry out their contract or refund the money which the municipality of Inverness paid them and which they accepted under false pretenses and with evident intention of disregarding their obligation with respect to that portion of the road from Inverness North. The people of Inverness, I am convinced, would accept the refund gladly, provided the Government would construct the Orangedale-Cheti-camp railroad which would be a much moTe desirable solution of the railway question in Inverness. I will have something to say on this later on, when the Railway Estimates are being considered.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: How much did they pay?

I could not tell my
right hon. friend exactly, but I know that they gave them $1,000 a mile bonus and a free right of way through for the most part rich agricultural lands under good cultivation, where this road wrought great damage to property in form of residences and buildings of various kinds, most valuable meadows and fields in a high state of cultivation. The exact amount paid for the right of way can be had from the treasurer of the county. It will be found to have been a very substantial amount.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Was there any date fixed within which the extension should be made?

The answer to this question can be found in the Nova Scotia statutes, and even if there is no time limit in the statute the agreement between

the company and the municipality will show without a doubt what the conditions of the payment of the bonus were, and what the obligations of the company were with Tespeet to the extension of the road to Cheticamp. The Inverness Railway and Coal Company got their charter from what is known as the Inverness and Richmond Railway Company. There were dates fixed for the construction of the line to Broad Cove, now called Inverness, and on the completion of the road to Broad cove the company agreed to construct the road to Cheticamp forthwith, provided Dominion and local subsidies were available. The Dominion and local subsidies were available. My predecessor had the subsidy of $6,400 brought down, and when I took charge I had this subsidy Te-voted. Mackenzie, Mann and Company could have got the subsidies at any time, and the Legislature of Nova Scotia was ready to pay them a subsidy of $4,000 a mile. I am satisfied that Mackenzie, Mann and Company would build that road, because it is a first-class proposition, but what they want is first to get hold of all the coal in North Inverness. But while Mackenzie, Mann and Company are endeavouring to carry out their own selfish plans, endeavouring to get control of all this coal, the people of Inverness are without railway accommodation and their natural resources are left undeveloped. They will be left in this undeveloped condition until Mackenzie, Mann and Company get hold of all the coal in North Inverness at their own price, unless the Government compel them to build the read forthwith or refund the money. The Government can do this if they so desire; but my suggestion is that the Government cause Mackenzie and Mann to refund the municipality of Inverness subventions, and construct the Intercolonial Railway branch line from Orangedale to Cheticamp, which is the correct business way of solving our railway question in North Inverness. It will give us railway accommodation^ that will not be under the control of a selfish corporation like Mackenzie and Mann. An Intercolonial Railway branch line is much more likely to stimulate the development of our natural resources than a road under the control of Mackenzie and Mann. Particularly will this apply to our coal wealth at St. Rose and Chimney Corner, our fishing industry and our farming industry.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The difficulty, as I explained to my hon. friend (Mr. A. W. Chisholm) on Wednesday last, is that this
is partly a coal proposition and partly a railway undertaking. As far as I can understand, the coal enterprise forms the larger part of it and it seems undesirable to bring the coal enterprise . into a proposition of this kind. It did not seem to me that should be done.	For
that reason we do not propose to bring that road in at the present time, although there is provision in the Bill by which the railway part at least can be brought in hereafter. My hon. friend may be assured that we will give careful attention to what he has represented in that regard. I agree with him that there is a very great opportunity in that part of the country for an enormous development in the coal industry.
I know that a flourishing town has already been built up-the town of Inverness, tnat I had the pleasure of visiting -about four years ago, where I found prosperous communities gathered around these mines. I am not aware whether the coal mine operations are profitable or whether they are fairly self-sustaining.
They have -been somewhat profitable of late years.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
But we did not want to bring a coal-mining proposition into an arrangement of this kind. It may be possible to separate the railway part and the coal mining part of the enterprise. It is a subject that requires some consideration. My hon. friend may be assured that we will give it the best consideration we can, and I shall ibe glad to discuss the matter privately with him should it be convenient for him to do so.
Mr. PUGS'LEY: I think that my hon. friend from Inverness (Mr. A. W. Chisholm) has given a pretty good answer to the Solicitor General as regards the Inverness Railway and -Coal 'Company. Now, I w-ant to make -a reply to my hon. friend in regard to the right to withdraw the land in the townsites. The Solicitor General says that the Canadian Northern Railway Company -are to convey all their property to the Government, and this makes the Government entirely safe, or as safe as it can be made, in respect to the townsites That is not the case, because all these townsites mentioned! in the third schedule, in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, and there are, I suppose, 200 or 300 of them, including the townsite of Port Mann in British Columbia, are declared to be owned by Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, and not by the Can-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: Mr. Chair-12 noon. man-
I want to hear the Postmaster General.

The hon. gentleman may hear from the Postmaster General also. I do not think he would want me to sit down. I desire to commend the industry with which my hon. friend has dug into the trust deed of 1913 to find something which will weaken the security which the Government now takes, which weakness he says we should cure. I must regret, on behalf of the bondholders who loaned their money on the strength of this trust deed, that they had not the discretion to engage the hon. member for St. John as their counsel in the matter, to see that they got some security and that the trust deed held down the so-called buccaneers, Messrs. Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited.

Since September 12 there has been in progress in the mines of the Canadian 'Collieries in British -Columbia, which are owned and controlled, I understand, iby Mackenzie and Mann, a labour strike which has not yet .been settled. I wish to bring to the attention of the Government, particularly of the Department of Labour, that that strike is still going on, and that the Canadian 'Collieries, Limited, so far have made no attempt to give the employees of that colliery a fair and equitable settlement of their grievances. It will be remembered that, in the session of 1911-12, this Government took the ground that where companies were looking for benefits from this Government, and where those companies were not treating their employees rightly, the Government w'ould come to the assistance of the employees and refuse to pass the legislation which these companies were requesting. This was done, if we are to
believe a speech of the Minister of Labour delivered in this House in this session, in connection with the Grand Trunk Railway Company. He told us at that time that the Grand Trunk Railway Company refused to take back certain of their employees after a settlement had been effected by the Labour Department of the late Government, and that, to make that settlement effective and binding, this Parliament and this Government refused to grant to the Grand Trunk Railway Company certain legislation which they were then promoting. If the Minister of Labour and the Department of Labour of this Government were successful in bringing back into the employ of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, men who had been illegally and unjustifiably debarred from their, labour on that system, then I think it is incumbent upon the Government in this present instance to do something to settle the strike in the Canadian collieries at Cumberland and Ladysmith. I believe it can be easily done. This Government have set a precedent in a matter of this kind in connection with the Grand Trunk strike. In justice to the labour men of this country, and particularly to the labour men of the Canadian collieries at Cumberland and Ladysmith, in British Columbia, they should do the same thing there. I am bringing this matter to the attention of the Government, and particularly of the Department of Labour, at this juncture, and asking them to make some attempt to bring those parties together so that they will reach a settlement; and I may say if that settlement is not forthcoming before the resolutions leave the committee, I shall move an amendment to the resolutions. My object this morning is simply to bring this matter to the attention of the Government.

In the mean- . time, I should like more explanation than we have had as to the full meaning of this subsection. It says that we arc to have a mortgage on all the .securities which are mentioned in the trust deed of the 30th of June, 1903, and those mentioned in the second part of the schedule. There are others to come hereafter, I imagine, and no indication has been given up to tilie present time what they arc. It is evident that the trust-deed of the 30th June, 1903, is a part of this agreement. It would 'be clearer if that were explained. I know it was placed on the table, and I had it for a few hours, but lent it to some friend and have not seen it since. It is evidently complicated. Perhaps the hon. Solicitor General will tell us what these are which are mentioned in the second schedule of Part II.

The securities covered
by section b which is now under discussion, are named in Part II of the second schedule. They include chiefly bonds of

allied companies, or of subsidiary companies, and also stocks of these companies -not in all cases stocks, for reasons which I can explain in each individual case. These companies were formed for the purpose of handling certain interests that were of value to the railway company. For example, the Winnipeg Land Company handles lands in Winnipeg that are occupied for railway purposes now. These lands were acquired in the early days at very low prices. The Winnipeg Land Company, in order to assist the Canadian Northern railway to secure the money needed, in 1903 bonded its assets for the sum mentioned here. $300,000, and issued stock for $100,000. The Canadian Northern railway took these bonds and these stocks. The proceeds of the bonds went to discharge what was against the land company-the cost of the properties of the company. The stocks and the bonds became the property of the Canadian Northern railway, and all that went out of the treasury of the Canadian Northern railway except for its own purposes went to discharge what was against the Winnipeg Land Company in the cost of its properties. Now, I will follow that individual case and see what security we have in virtue of this clause. The stocks and the bonds, are brought in and become part of the mortgage under the trust deed of the 30th June, 1903, which secured the four per cent perpetual bond issue. That trust deed provides that the company shall be able to exercise its power to acquire the bonds of other companies, and for every $100 bond it shall acquire it shall have power to issue another $100 perpetual bond, secured in the same way as the first issue of four per cent perpetual debenture bonds. That is quite clear to me, and I hope I have made it equally clear to the committee. This security ranks equal with that in all respects. Consequently, the company is still able to issue four per cent perpetual debenture bonds, and no issue they have made since the first issue in any way impairs the security of the subsequent issues. Consequently we secure by this subsection a mortgage on the equity of redemption, the right, so far as the property of these companies is concerned, to go ahead of all other issues. That is to say, we secure a mortgage on all the assets of the company and put our mortgage in that form so that there will be no way of any assets escaping. And, while there is an issue against each issue of four per cent perpetual debenture stock, it is 
secured also by the further assets of the company. The purpose of the clause is to provide that the trustee of the new trust deed shall have security on all the equity that there is or that there may be.

This section
says:
Grant a specific mortgage or charge upon the mortgage securities and shares of stock now or hereafter from time to time deposited with and specifically mortgaged under the trust deed of the 30th day of June, 1903.
We have here a mortgage of all that comes into the trust deed or will come into it hereafter. Then the section says that what we now have is all the mortgages that are mentioned in the second part of schedule 2, that is to say, the Minnesota and Ontario Bridge Company, the Minnesota and Manitoba Railway Company, Lake Superior Terminals Company, Limited, Canadian Northern Telegraph Company, Winnipeg Land Company, Limited, The Canadian Northern Coal and Ore Dock Company, the St. Boniface and Western Land Company, the Edmonton and Slave Lake Railway Company, Canadian Northern Railway Express Company, Limited, Canadian Northern Steamships, Limited, Canadian Northern System Terminals, Limited. These are the securities mentioned in this section. If I interpreted the explanation of my hon. friend aright, it is this: no other companies can come in except those which are the proceeds of these companies or which may be taken in by other companies or be replaced by other securities. Am I right?

I do not say that no
other bonds or other companies may come in; they may come in. What I said is that under our mortgage no other companies can come in ahead of us.

I understand
that. The section says:
Those now so deposited and mortgaged being mentioned in the second part of the said second schedule.
But there are others which may from time to time come in. Which are they?
There are none in contemplation now, so far as I know. That refers to such bonds as the company may think it wise to purchase for the purposes of the road.
Would it not be clearer and safer to have the trust deed of 1903 made part of these resolutions.

I do not think that any object could be served by incorporating the trust deed as part of the resolution; we ara directly interested in only one portion of it, in so far as it covers this issue. We provide that we come next after the security formed by the trust deed o_f 1903.

In respect of the fourth item on page 30 of the blue-book, the 4 per cent debenture stock guaranteed by Alberta, $6,776,000, would the Solicitor General have prepared, at as early a date as convenient, a clear statement showing the direct proceeds of this and the indirect proceeds that my hon. friend has spoken of-the proceeds being much larger than the securities issued- also the same particulars in regard to numbers 21 and 22, debenture stocks guaranteed by the province of Alberta. In the case of numbers 21 and 22, the stock and bonds guaranteed are those of the Canadian Northern Western railway, while in the case of number 4, it is the Canadian Northern railway. I am anxious for a statement which will separate these securities distinctly and completely.

I think that can be
procured.

The mortgage upon the Canadian Northern and its properties is practically the only physical asset, outside of the securities upon certain stocks, which the country is getting as security under this agreement. From that point of view, it is very important to ascertain how much equipment is free from the equipment trust.
I have asked for that.
I assume that only tlie equipment of the Canadian Northern railway will be covered by the mortgage.
The mortgage will cover all the equipment that is clear and the equity of the Canadian Northern in such that may be subject to the equipment trust.

At this stage the
Solicitor General ought to take the committee into his confidence as to what further security, if any, the Government has sought to obtain from the contractors to whom this money is to be advanced. I assume that the Government would be actuated by the idea that they should obtain all the security of every kind that it is possible to obtain. Have the Government asked any of the members of the firm of Mackenzie, Mann and Company to put up any of their personal property as security? Did they ask them to give what was sought from the Canadian Pacific railway directors in 1884? Did they seek, in addition to that, to obtain any security other than what is contained in section 2?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What is the security to which my hon. friend alludes as having been given in 1884?

It is understood that in 1884 the men who were interested in the Canadian Pacific railway at that time pledged their own personal guarantee, if not in the formal arrangement with the Government, at least antecedent to their coming to the Government for aid. The aid that was given by the Government at that time was given only after the absorption of the personal finances of the men who were connected with the road. Hon. gentlemen who have taken part in the previous discussion of this measure have urged upon the Government the point that the personal properties and assets of these gentlemen should be given as security under this agreement. Have the Government endeavoured to obtain that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am not aware that any securities were given to the Government in 1884 by the individual shareholders or directors of the Canadian Pacific railway. It is quite possible that they may have pledged their assets to banks for the purpose of assisting the road, and I always understood, without any exact knowledge on the point, that previously to that date such was the case. As a matter of fact, I am perfectly satisfied that the liability of those who hold the shares in this railway has been pledged to a very large amount in connection with its construction. In addition to that, as my hon. friend has already observed, and as has been pointed out in the discussion, we have exacted three stipulations in connection with this arrangement which, I think, were not exacted in 1884. In the first place, we have provided by section 4 of the Bill that the current indebtedness, or floating liabilities, which run up to nearly $11,000,000, shall be reduced to the normal amount of $3,000,000; that Mackenzie and Manm, Limited, shall give security for that, and that they shall be obliged to give to the Government such other securities as the Governor in Council may require. We have also asked them to furnish satisfactory security, which must be

given before the bonds are guaranteed, that all outstanding temporary loans against which securities have been pledged shall be taken care of and that no prooeediing shall be taken against the road in respect of those loans. Thus neither the floating indebtedness nor the temporary loans will embarrass the company in the operation of the portions of the line already completed or during the construction of those that remain to be completed. Then, in addition to that, we have asked them to forego >aR claims, which we believe might have been enforced to a very large -amount, against the road for agency services and otherwise. In that regard it seems to me that we have gone much further than the -Government went in 1884 or than any government has since gone.

I think there is a wide margin for difference of opinion as to the last .statement of my right hon. friend. It is a matter of record, certainly it is well known, that in 1884 the promoters of the Canadian Pacific railway, chiefly George Stephen and Donald Smith of that day, pledged their own personal credit to the fullest amount in order to carry out the enterprise. They could not get anything more from the banks that had carried the enterprise, as the banks did not feel warranted in giving any further assistance; they could not get any money to finish the enterprise and they came to the Government. There is little reason to believe that those who pledged personally their credit to the banks would not have pledged it to the Government if the Government had so required. The Government did not at that time require the personal securities of George Stephen tod Donald Smith and the ether promoters, for the sufficient reason that the company was able to give of its own securities sufficient to fully guarantee the loan of $30,000,000. The best evidence of that was that the loan was paid in due time and according to stipulation. The best justification, as I have said, was that the iloan was repaid in due time by those to whom it had been made, the company. In this case the Government has not taken, any personal pledge from Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann, although it may be true that Mackenzie and Mann, as stated by my hon. friend, had pledged their credit to their creditors. But if Mackenzie and Mann have .pledged their personal credit to their creditors, there is no reason in the world to suppose that they would

not have done as much for the Government as they have done for their creditors, and there is every reason why the Government should have been as prudent as the other creditors of Mackenzie and Mann and should have exacted the same personal security from them. My right hon. friend says he has taken -ample securities. I do not think he can convince any man who has given the matter any .attention that the security is .at all. adequate to the amount of responsibility which we are taking. This is the reason why, as said by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), we ought not to he satisfied to take only the security of the company, but should have secured also the personal security of the promoters of the company, Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If I am not mistaken, a colleague of my right hon. friend, in 1909, in dealing with another matter, described the securities taken by the Government in 1884 as valueless at the time, as a security which could not be realized upon in any bank in the country, but as one which eventually did turn out as fully adequate for the reason that the road became a success. I think the security which we are taking at this time is fully equal to that which the Government took in 1884; and, further than that, I say that we have imposed upon the persons who are the promoters of this road very much larger obligations in connection with this guarantee than were imposed in 1884. I have already pointed them out and I need not Tepeat them. I find nothing of that kind in 1884 and I s-ay that it is beyond question, in connection with the construction of this road, that Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann have pledged their personal credit for the purpose of raising money to provide for the construction, to as -large an amount at least- as was pledged by any person associated with the Canadian Pacific railway in 1884 or previously to that time. But we have not been satisfied with that; we have asked them to take care of the obligations to which I have alluded and to take care that the floating indebtedness shall not be brought against the road and shall be reduced within, a year from $10,500,000 or $11,000,000 to $3,000,000. We have asked them to provide security that the temporary loans shall be taken care of. They will be largely taken care of, perhaps not altogether, by the securities pledged against them; but if there is any deficiency, and there might be a deficiency of a considerable amount under conceivable circumstan-

ces, they are bound to give their security that they will take care of it.

The people who
undertake to do these things are not Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann; they are the joint stock company known as Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, so that there is no personal liability involved.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We have been told in
this House that a very large proportion of the assets of Mackenzie and Mann are .vested in that company. If so, all those assets become liable.
The total capitalization is only $5,000,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It may be only $5,000,-
000, but whether it be large or small we are entitled, under the stipulations of this contract as embodied in the fourth and fifth sections of the Bill, to require further securities which must be to the satisfaction of the Government.

Could the hon. member tell the committee what are the assets of Mackenzie and Mann, Limited? We have heard a good deal of comment by my hon. friend and the Solicitor General as to the assurance of Mackenzie and Mann being given that these floating liabilities and also these loans from the banks would be taken care of. In answer to a question by myself, the right hon. gentleman stated that, under clauses 4 and 5, they have the power to see that other securities shall be given; and they seem to want to lead the country and the House to believe that these floating liabilities and bank loans will be taken care of. We are only repeating, we have gone over the ground; but the hon. member for Pictou and other gentlemen have pointed out that there is no personal liability here, no promise by anybody excepting Mackenzie and Mann, Limited, and we have no knowledge whether Mackenzie and Mann, Limited, own a dollar or not. The Government should be in a position to let us know whether Mackenzie and Mann, Limited, are of any financial value, or whether they are simply an organized company. They say that the stock is $5,000,000. But the stock is of no value, the question is. What property have they? I would like to know what assets they have behind the stock. Could not the minister tell us? I think he ought to take the committee into his confidence and tell us what securities or guarantees he is going to require other than the guarantee of the contractor, which
means Mackenzie and Mann, and whether Sir Wfiliam Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann will become personally responsible.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It means that we shall
scrutinize very carefully whatever obligations are given to us to fulfil the conditions set forth in the fourth and fifth sections of the Bill; and we shall make ourselves and do make ourselves responsible to Parliament and to the country to see that the security is satisfactory and will fulfil the purpose for which it is designed.
As far as the assets of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, are concerned, I am not in a position to enumerate them all, and it is not necessary that I should do so, because we are not obliged to confine ourselves to the security of that company, and we do not propose to confine ourselves to that company unless we are thoroughly satisfied with it. We know that they own the stock and .bonds in the Townsites Company subject to the securities outstanding.
About $20,000,000 outstanding.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I understand there would be an equity of a very considerable amount; at least, we are so disposed to regard it on the basis of the figures I have already given to the House. Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, also own the stock of the Canadian Northern railway. Outside of that I cannot say exactly what they own; they have some real estate, I understand.

My hon. friend has left the matter exactly where it was before he attempted to answer. If he will not give the committee any further information, we have no way of compelling him to do so. He says that they will make a very careful examination and satisfy themselves whether Mackenzie and Mann have sufficient assets to make their guarantee of any value, and then he says: We will have to take the responsibility. My right hon. friend takes the responsibility, and says that he knows these debts will be paid. But what if they are not? Why not have somebody brought ,in who we know is responsible? Sir William Mackenzie we know is responsible, and well able to pay whatever depreciation there may be in the securities put out by the different companies as against floating indebtedness and bank loans. If the Premier would say that Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann would personally be held responsible, we would

feel the country was getting some sort oi protection. I believe I am voicing the sentiments of members on this side of the House, and I know it is the feeling of thousands and tens of thousands in this country, when I say that, for some inconceivable reason, the Government is not taking the House and the country into its confidence over this particular phase of the Bill. When these gentlemen come here for this enormous guarantee of $45,000,000, very likely to be followed by another guarantee within the next year, or so, why does the Government absolutely refuse to make Mackenzie and Mann personally liable? That is something the country cannot understand. It is all very nice for my right hon. friend to say: We take the responsibility. We appreciate that, but it is like locking the door after the horse is stolen. My right hon. friend takes the responsibility but it will be perhaps two or three years before the House and the country knows whether or not the security is sufficient to pay the debts, and if it turns out that the security is not sufficient and they come back here in another year or two for further assistance, it is poor consolation for the people to be told: We took the responsibility; it is true we had power in our hands to make Mackenzie and Mann responsible, but we thought it was hardly fair to crowd them, as they are great empire builders, magnates and all that sort of thing; it is unfortunate the securities were not sufficient. But that will not help the country. If my right hon. friend would go a little further and tell the House what additional security he proposes asking in addition to the security of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, it would be much more satisfactory to the House and the country.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I hope my hon. friend
does not think I am declining to take him into my confidence, for there is no reason why I should not give him the fullest possible confidence on this point. As far as the taking of security is concerned, I can assure my hon. friend that it was not based on any consideration of empire builders, but on strict business principles. The whole question will be dealt with from the standpoint that the Government under this Bill is entitled to receive, and will certainly exact, security that will be regarded as good security upon the strictest business principles. That is how we propose to deal with it. My hon. friend will realize that it is impossible to deal with such matters as the value of a security and all details

of security in a committee of this House. In such matters something must be entrusted to the executive, and we intend to carry out our duty in that regard in. the strictest possible manner.

I give my right hon.
friend credit for being sincere in his statement that he intends to do what is right. He has heard, though, of the old adage that the way to a certain place is paved with good intentions, and it may be that this will be another stone in the pavement. Would my hon. friend consider me impertinent if I were to ask whether,in the negotiations leading up to this, the Government really asked Mackenzie and Mann to be personally responsible for a portion of these liabilities?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We certainly did, otherwise we should not have got the stipulations embodied in sections 4 and 5 of the resolutions.
They are not personally liable.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, are.
But not Mackenzie and Mann personally.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We have the power under sections 4 and 5, if we deem it necessary to exercise it, of asking Mackenzie and Mann or both to become responsible.

But it does not say they will, and that is just the difficulty. The country would like to know whether in these negotiations Mackenzie and Mann were asked to be personally responsible and whether they refused to become responsible under sections 4 and 5. Let my right hon. friend face the matter for a moment from the standpoint of a man on the outside. Suppose we pass sections 4 and 5 exactly as they stand. My right hon. friend investigates the securities which Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, offer, and he becomes satisfied that that company have not sufficient assets to make their guarantee of any value. Then my right hon. friend asks Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann personally to sign a guarantee. Suppose they refuse, what can my right hon. friend do? He may say: Oh, well, we will not go on with the deal then. But I want to tell my right hon. friend that he cannot refuse to go on with the deal. Mackenzie and Mann will have him in the hollow of their hands as abso-

lutely as one man ever had another, because the whole ground on which my right hon. friend asks for this legislation is the ground that the Canadian Northern railway is bankrupt; that its promoters are up against a stone wall; that they exhausted every possible means of financing their great enterprise and cannot go any further, and that the only place to which they can come for assistance is the Parliament of Canada. Suppose Parliament passes sections 4 and 5 whereby Mackenzie and Mann can be asked personally to become responsible. If Mackenzie and Mann refuse and say they will not give that guarantee, my right hon. friend has no option but to take what they will give him. That is the great objection I have to this clause. I would like to see it put in the Bill that Mackenzie and Mann are personally responsible to pay these two items. I am not arguing now that they should be made responsible for the whole 145,000,000, because these sections 4 and 5 do not refer to the $45,000,000; they are not supposed to, although they do in the end, I think. They refer to the reduction of floating liabilities and to making good certain loans outstanding against which security has been pledged as collateral. We are asking that Mackenzie and Mann should be personally liable for those items. Personally, I think they should be made responsible for the whole $45,000,000, because after all we are putting up the money to protect their property. Why should they not; we are putting up the money to protect their property? They have come to the end of their rope, they cannot go anywhere else for money, they have come to us, and to avert a national calamity we are compelled to put up the money. Why should they not become personally responsible for the whole thing? Outside of the question of principle, this is really the crucial point of this matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I know we have the right to call upon Mackenzie, Mann and Company under sections 4 and 5 of the resolutions to give the security to which my hon.
friend alludes.
Mr. CARVELL; Do I understand my right hon. friend to say that we do not have the right?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I say we have the right absolutely when we desire to exercise it. We are not concerned about Mackenzie and Mann giving it, we are concerned about
some person giving an absolutely sufficient safe security to the Government that these two stipulations will be carried out. If we got a security from a large bank it might be a great deal better than that which Mackenzie and Mann could give us, and we might be satisfied with that. But the main point is that the security must be satisfactory. When my hon. friend enlarges upon the importance of these gentlemen giving their own personal security, I want to recur again to 1884 when that course was not taken in regard to the shareholders and directors of the Canadian Pacific railway. When, in 1911, the late Administration guaranteed the bonds of the Canadian Northern railway to the amount of $35,000,001, no security whatever was taken outside of a mortgage upon the road. My hon. friend retorts at once that that was a first mortgage and that this is not a first mortgage. I am prepared to show, and can show, that the charge which we obtain upon the Canadian Northern railway and its allied enterprises under this resolution is very little larger per mile than that which was accepted by the late Administration in 1911, and I am also prepared to show that the road upon which we are taking security now is, at present, and for many years will be, mile for mile, a very much better security than that which was accepted in 1911. We have not stood where my hon. friend and his leader stood in 1911. We have required not only that security, but the other securities which are enumerated in the resolution, and we have required also that security aggregating more than $27,000,000 shall be given to the satisfaction of the Government, and under such stipulations that Mackenzie. Mann and Company, if necessary, can be asked to make themselves individually responsible.

My right hon. friend
has a wonderful faculty of delving into ancient history when he wants .to get away from an unpleasant situation. We have had very many illustrations in the last two and a half years of my right bon. friend's desire to shield himself behind what somebody else did, usually my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). Now he goes back and shields himself behind Sir John Macdonald. It ia all very well for my right hon. friend to try and get away from the real question that I have propounded to him and. which he has not answered. Of course, 1 have no means of compelling him to,
423a

answer these two questions, but the House and the committee would like to havei him answer them. The first is: Has anybody ever asked Mackenzie and Mann to become personally responsible for these liabilities? and the second question is: What is my right hon. friend going to do if later on he asks Mackenzie and Mann to be responsible under sections 4 and 5 and they refuse? Where has he anything in these resolutions upon which the Bill will be founded by which he can compel Mackenzie and Mann to come in and become personally responsible if they refuse to do so? Will he not be compelled to pay the $45,000,000 if they do refuse? This is boiling the matter down to the important point, and I think that my right hon. friend should not talk about ancient history, about what Sir John Macdonald and my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition did, but he should tell us what he is going to do undeT these particular conditions.
The hon. gentleman was not present when ancient history was gone into on the other side of the House.
Oh, yes, I was.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We were confronted with the example of what was done in 1884-
I was here.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
And that is the reason
why I alluded to it. I thought it was always safe to offer a good example to my hon. friend and therefore I also alluded to what was done in 1911, knowing that it would commend itself to his good judgment as a perfectly wise and prudent course. To-day he will not find fault with me for suggesting to him what I regard as a good example, not by way of tu quoque, but sirnpy for the sake of a valuable precedent. My hon. friend asks what we would do to-day if Mackenzie and Mann refused to carry out some of the conditions precedent to the guarantee? My hon. friend might as well ask what we would do if they refused to sign this agreement because it is a condition precedent.

But Mackenzie, Mann
and Company, Limited, have agreed to sign the agreement.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There is no stipulation
oi that kind. My hon. friend might as well ask what would we do if they refused to execute the trust deed to the satisfaction of the Government. What would we do if

they refused to carry out the stipulations of subsection c, and What would we; do if they refused to transfer to the Minister of Finance and the Receiver General the stock? All these things are conditions precedent and so, in the Bill which we propose to found upon this resolution, sections 4 and 5 will be made conditions precedent. Thus it is useless to propound an inquiry like that. My hon. friend knows that the Canadian Northern railway have come to us and asked us to give assistance under certain conditions. We have fixed what the conditions shall be and before we give that assistance these conditions must be complied with. If they refuse to comply .with these conditions we cannot give the assistance.

Nobody assumes that
my right hon. friend or the Government would have introduced these resolutions without having some sort of an arrangement made with Mackenzie, Mann and Company. We take it for granted that everything in regard to the resolutions has been agreed upon by Mackenzie, Mann and Company or by the Canadian Northern Railway Company. If that be not the case it is a hundred times worse than I thought it was. It is bad enough as it is and we do not want to make it any worse. I do not think that my right hon. friend can get very much comfort by arguing in that way and saying: What will happen if Mackenzie, Mann and Company refuse to hand over the securities? We take it for granted that that has been agreed upon. Now, would my tight hon. friend be equally frank and tell me whether in the negotiations they have ever asked Mackenzie and Mann to be personally responsible or whether it is their intention to ask Mackenzie and Mann to become personally responsible under sections 4 and 5 in case they are satisfied that the other security offered is not sufficient to meet the guarantee?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have already explained to my hon. friend that sections 4 and 5 embrace the general scope which would authorize us to call upon Mackenzie, Mann and Company to become personally liable and, of course, my hon. friend is quite right in one sense in saying that the Canadian Northern Railway Company agreed to these conditions. Perhaps that is not precisely the best way of putting it. They did not exactly agree to them, but they ascertained they could not get any assistance

except upon the conditions set out in these resolutions.
That is an agreement.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The same thing.

No agreement has
been signed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No agreement has been signed; we did not think it worth while until Parliament authorized it. But it was submitted to Mackenzie, Mann and Company, and they were told that the agreement must be signed before the securities are guaranteed. That is made a condition precedent. .
Was it explained that Mackenzie, Mann and Company could personally be brought under sections 4 and 5?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It was perfectly understood that if we should require Mackenzie, Mann and Company to be guarantors under sections 4 and 5 they would do so.
Is it the right hon. the Premier's intention to ask Mackenzie and Mann to become responsible personally under sections 4 and 5, in ease the other securities offered seem inadequate?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We shall certainly do so unless they offer us other security which is as good or better.

The condition to
which my right hon. friend refers and the action of the Government in regard to asking for other securities would only arise in the event of the $10,000,000 of current liabilities not being disposed of, or does my right hon. friend mean to say that these guarantees of a personal character would be asked for at the time of the making of the trust deed?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
These are all conditions
precedent to the exaction of the securities in connection with which the trust deed will 'be executed. I do not know whether I gather the purport of my hon. friend's question,

My right hon. friend was referring to sections 4 and 5. Section 4 relates to the undertaking, namely, that the securities which are now pledged with the banks of the country will be made available solely for the purpose of paying off the hanks. Section 5 is the one by which the contractors undertake that the liabilities, known as current liabilities which are to be found on page 43 of the
blue-book, amounting to $10,408,000, will be retired. My right hon. friend has intimated that the Government may resort to the personal securities of Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann in order to see that that is done. Does he mean to say that that resorting will be made at the time of the signing of the trust deed, or later on at the end of the year?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Before we guarantee any securities at all. There are two items to which my hon. friend has alluded. One is the reduction of the current or floating indebtedness, which is nearly $8,000,000 in excess of what it should be. I understand that has run up, to some extent but not altogether, owing to the payments on rolling stock equipment. We insisted that that should be taken care of to our satisfaction, and reduced to its normal amount of $3,000,000 within one year; and that in the meantime no proceedings should be taken. We have the right to call upon Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann to become personally responsible for that; and as I said before, we shall do so unless they offer us as good or better security. The same is true with regard to what is called the temporary loans. Here is a very considerable amount, in the vicinity of $20,000,000, which is secured by the pledge of certain securities which were not saleable at a reasonable price. These securities may probably realize the whole or the greater part of that loan; but in any event we are bound to have absolutely satisfactory security that no claim shall be made; that Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann shall take care of it.

If I rightly understand the conversation which has just taken place between my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell) and my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, and the assurance with which that conversation has been concluded, I should like to 4 p.m. say, in my judgment, that assurance will relieve a great deal of natural and justifiable anxiety which exists in western Canada in regard to this whole transaction. As far as I know the opinion of the West, there is no hostility to this road, I think we may trust the communications which the Prime Minister has brought before this House from the acting Premier of Saskatchewan and the Prime Minister of Alberta as being very good evidence that there is no hostility to the road, but there is wide-spread and deep-seated

distrust of the men who have been connected with the road. that distrust is founded upon the belief, very widely held amongst the people, that these men individually and personally own timber limits, real estate, coal mines, newspapers and other forms of personal property, which they can have gained, in the minds of the man in the street, only by a diversion of the moneys which should have gone into the building of the railroad. If I rightly understand my right hon. friend, he has given us the assurance that, in so far as the Government is concerned, any property which these men hold in their individual capacity will be called upon, if need be.
Oh, no.
I understood my right hon. friend in that sense.
No.

Then the anxiety is not
removed. That is what is troubling the people in the West. I am not a lawyer and I am not of the class to which Burns refers when he speaks about people eking out their common sense by law. But that is what I understand as a layman.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think my hon.
friend is substantially right. As far as making money out of these roads is concerned, we have had a pTetty careful examination made by the most expert auditors in the Government service, and they have satisfied us that no money has been diverted. They were instructed to make a very careful and detailed examination, and further than that, they were instructed, if they found themselves incapable of dealing with the situation, that they were at liberty to employ Price, Waterhouse and Company or any other great accounting firm to assist them. We found from their report that there was no ground for suspicion that any portion of the money had been diverted. We found, however, that there was the probability of a very large claim for agency services; and we insisted that that claim should be absolutely released, not only by Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, but by Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann. In addition to that, apart from the items connected with the construction of the road which were placed before us in the first instance showing a deficiency of $42,000,000 which would require to be raised, we ascertained that there were two other items which might prove troublesome and- em-

barrassing to the project of completing the road. One of those was an item of about $8,000,000 of excess current or floating indebtedness; the other was an item of $20,000,000 and upwards which was secured by the pledge of bonds and similar securities which were not saleable at a reasonable price. We have exacted two stipulations. One is that no proceedings shall be taken against the road for any part of that sum of $8,000,000, and that it shall be cleared off in the space of one year; and we have the right under this contract to exact from Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann their personal security in that respect, and we shall exact it unless we get as good or better security.
So far as the other item of temporary loans is concerned, we have also exacted security to the satisfaction of the Government that no claim in respect to that shall .be made; that it shall be taken care of by the securities that are pledged for it, and that, if those securities are not sufficient, the additional securities which are given to us shall take care of it. In that way and to that extent my hon. friend is quite night in the view which he has taken of the effect of the arrangement.

Just to have the record perfectly plain, I want to inform my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) that we on this side of the House would be only too happy if the Premier would extend his promise to all the liabilities and to the repayment of the $45,000,000 advanced. I am afraid that was the idea which my hon. friend from Red Deer obtained from listening to the discussion between my right hon. friend and myself. Unhappily such is not the case.
I started out by stating a doubt as to my own understanding.

If my hon. friend will look at pages 44 and 45 of the blue-book, he will find, at page 44, that about $15,423,000 has been loaned to the Canadian Northern system, which i.s secured by collateral of certain kinds, and that the collateral appears to be very much in excess of the loan. We have grave dounte about that collateral being capable of taking care of the loans. Turning to page 45, schedule b, these, as I understand, are loans advanced by the banks amounting to $20,703,865.

That amount includes
all the loans. I do not know what the

$15,000,000 is to -which the hon. gentleman refers.
Those given on page 44. Part of that list is in currency and part in sterling. Reducing the sterling to our currency I -make the total $15,423,070.

That is not a separate debt at all. That is -a part of the whole indebtedness included in the $312,000,000. That schedule was made to show such securities as were only pledged as collateral, and not directly realized upon.
