If one takes the $312,000,000 and the $20,700,000, he has everything that has been raised on the strength of the securities. This amount in schedule (-a) is not an extra amount.

I have 'been labouring under an impression that in some way section four of the resolution provided for the payment of these loans. If not I am giving the Solicitor General credit for more than he ought to have. However, he will agree that these loans of $20,700,000 are covered by the terms of section four of the resolution.
Yes.
I supposed, of course, these amounts at page 44 were covered also. It is getting worse.
I did not say that.
One moment.
The hon. gentleman is-

The Solicitor General
will have his turn.
Mr. MEIGHEN-arguing from a false hypothesis. However, he does not mind that.

The hon. gentleman will 'have full opportunity to make an answer to the point raised by my hon, friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark). In addition there is something like $11,000,000 on current account which we are told ought to be $3,000,000, and under clause 5 of the resolution, the contractors, Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann are going to covenant that $8,000,000 of the $11,000,000 shall be paid. These aie the only amounts, as I understand, for which the Prime Minister has agreed he will hold Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann personally liable, hut he will not hold them for the payment of the $45,000,000. If the Prime Minister will go so far as to make these gentlemen- liable
for the $45,000,000 he will relieve the minds of hon. gentlemen on this -side very much.

The discussion, it seems to me, shows how this position may be completely summarized. We are not making Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald iManm personally parties to the agreement to refund the $45,000,000. But they must become parties to a covenant to repay the bank and -also to pay Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, the -Canadian Northern Railway Company, the Canadian Northern Ontario Railway Company, the Canadian Northern Quebec Railway Company, the Quebec and Bake St. John Railway Company, the Duluth, Winnipeg and Pacific Railway Company, the Halifax and Southwestern Railway Company, the Central Ontario Railway Company, -and all these other companies; and these companies, as shown by the correspondence and resolutions are owned by the Canadian Northern railway and by Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited,. AH these are to be paid by Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann personally, and the banks are to be given equal security, but the Dominion of Canada will not -look to these gentlemen- personally but to the Canadian Northern- railway and to Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We -are undertaking a
contingent liability as guarantors to the extent of $45,000,000, the sum estimated as necessary to -be guaranteed in order to raise the amount of $42,000,000 or thereabouts which will be required to complete the road. In the course of our investigation we have found other liabilities aggregating about $28,000,000 which have to be taken care of in order to insure the completion of the road. We exacted security from the gentlemen to provide for this $28,000,000, So far as $20,000,000 is concerned, that also is only a contingent liability, because the securities are pledged against it. As to the $8,000,000, that is a direct and absolute liability. In taking security from these gentlemen to provide for this $28,000,000, we have gone infinitely farther than any previous Government has ever gone in an engagement of this kind. We assume a contingent liability of $45,000,000, and Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann undertake the liability of $28,000,000 of which $20,000,000 is contingent.
What do they get for it ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: They do not get anything for it.
Does the right hon. gentleman mean to say that this will not be a charge against the system ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It will not become a charge against it any more than it is today. The securities have been pledged to the extent of $20,000,000 and this is a charge against the system. But, so far as the $8,000,000 is concerned, that is not a charge upon the system so far as I am aware.
No.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, that is a direct and absolute liability.

Then, if Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, are not sufficient security for the payment of the indebtedness of which he speaks, the Government intend to ask Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann to supplement that security with their own personal guarantee.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We might not be satisfied with the guarantee of Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann. What we demand is absolutely good security.

That is as I have already said. The Prime Minister insists on better security for the discharge of the debt to the banks and to the companies than for the discharge of the debt to the Government itself. He undertakes that Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann shall discharge these liabilities or shall have a delay for their reduction in the case of the companies to a normal amount. But the observation of my hon. friend from Red Deer still stands-that the Prime Minister should undertake to do for the country what he is doing for the banks and for Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The undertaking to
-which I have alluded runs up to $28,000,000. The contingent liability of $20,000,000 I have already explained. As to the liability of $8,000,000, I do not know how they are going to take care of it; I know that they have got to give satisfactory security. We intend to see that that amount is taken care of, that not one dollar of it shall come against the road to embarrass construction and that the whole $42,000,000 which is to be raised upon the guarantee of the country shall be devoted to the purposes that have already been explained.

I understand that the
obligations of the contractors are contained in sections 4 and 5, but they are merely liabilities either of the Canadian Northern or of the subsidiary companies. All that Mackenzie and Mann, Limited, seek to do is, in some way, to have what are called the floating liabilities reduced within one year. With regard to the liabilities that are to be paid out of the securities which are pledged for them, surely my right hon. friend gave a wrong impression -when he said that Mackenzie and Mann would take care of them, in the sense that they would assume and pay them themselves. They still remain obligations of this firm, of the Canadian Northern and of the Government of Canada. The people of Canada will owe two-fifths of them and Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, will owe three-fifths. If Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, have them taken care of in the meantime, they are to be paid out of the resources of the Canadian Northern railway, which is to be owned jointly by Mackenzie and Mann and the Government of Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In the same way that the indebtedness now proposed to be created will be the primary obligation of the Canadian Northern railway and will have to be paid by that railway. The country guarantees security, and will have to make it good if the Canadian Northern is unable to pay it, so the persons whom we call upon as guarantors in respect of the $28,000,000 will have to make it good unless the Canadian Northern is able to take care of it. The situations are precisely the same.

In other words, the
Government, as the owner of two-fifths of this undertaking, calls upon the people to guarantee an indebtedness of which two-fifths is now to be the debt of the people of Canada as owners of two-fifths of the capital stock. Mackenzie, Mann and Co. assume no liability upon their own part, but simply carry over the guarantee and liability of the company, which will be owed in the proportion of the country owing two-fifths and Mackenzie, Mann and Company owing three-fifths as shareholders for these amounts.

Would the Solicitor General, in order to make this matter clear, give us a succinct and clear statement as to what is the nature of the liability included in the statement set out on page 43

of the blue-book? For instance, the Canadian Northern Railway Company is said to owe $6,565,000. It is understood that that is due not to contractors or subcontractors and not for equipment or construction purposes, but for other purposes. What is it due for? What goes to make up these other items of indebtedness on the part of the subsidiary companies?

The item of $6,565,652.61 which appears on page 43 as part of the total floating liability or permanent indebtedness of the system, is part of $10,408,128.30. The debt of $6,565,000, to whicli the hon. member for Pictou refers, has arisen and is owing, I presume, largely to the banks. It has arisen because the company has been under the necessity of paying its equipment trusts out of current revenues. In that way the floating liabilities of the company have been increased, the equipment trusts including in each case not only the principal but interest. Hon. gentlemen will remember that, in the course of a speech delivered last week, I made that statement. I made definite inquiry from the auditor since, and I find that my statement was exactly correct. Just to whom it is owing in each case, I cannot say. It is not owiing to the holders of equipment trusts, because they have been paid, but it is owing to those from whom the money was secured to pay these equipment trusts. I do not say that that comprises the whole amount; I do not know what the normal indebtedness of the Canadian Northern probably would be: I presume that it is probably somewhere in the neighbourhood of a million and a half or two million. A road can never get rid of the whole of its floating liabilities, because station agents' balances and other accounts are coming in, and at the same time the accounts for the debts it owes are in many cases not rendered. These would include, of course, the ordinary current debts that a railway company incurs in the course of its business; these ordinary current debts would, from information which I have, run up, in the case of the Canadian Northern proper, to about $1,000,000 or $1,500,000. The balance will be comprised largely of indebtedness owing to those from whom it seemed the money to pay equipment trusts.

Is any part of the amount due for equipment trust purposes included in the statement found on page
42, where it is said that there is owing on general equipment account $1,539,000?

No; the item $1,539,863.87 appearing on page 42 as owing on general equipment is a part of the construction indebtedness of $21,262,527.26. It is owing on construction, and owing to the construction department of the road, Mackenzie and Mann, Limited, who in turn owe it to those from whom they purchased. It appears that the Canadian Northern Railway Company, as other railway companies do, find that they can purchase certain parts of their equipment more cheaply by purchasing them direct instead of having them purchased by car companies, manufactured into cars and then =old to the railway. It appears that the makers of bolsters and other such parts of railway cars will sell more cheaply to the railway companies, or to Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, who buy from the railway companies, than they will sell to the car companies. I am stating only what I am informed by the Railway Department is the experience of the Intercolonial. In that way they purchase certain of the equipment direct; that equipment is turned over to the car company, is included in the cars, and becomes part of the whole equipment, being sold first to the rolling stock company and then to the railway company. This $1,539,000 represents such amount of equipment as is bought direct from the construction department, Mackenzie, Mann and -Company, Limited.
But is not included in the $6,000,000 liability of the Canadian Northern mentioned on page 43?
No.
The Solicitor General is not clear as to what comprises this $6,000,000 of indebtedness except that it is in connection with equipment bonds.
And the ordinary current indebtedness of the company.

Of course in that
connection the Solicitor General might indicate to the committee whether or not his information would lead him to believe that it is expected that these equipment bonds would be sold and -that an amount of money would thereby be realized which would go back into the Canadian Northern Railway treasury and reduce its indebtedness. But take some of the other items; take the Canadian Northern Railway Quebec, one and a quarter millions. I think the hon. member

for Calgary, speaking of the Bay of Quinte item contained in the $10,000,000 list, said that that was the net loss on operation for a number of years. What other item in this list contains figures which are the net losses as well as the Bay of Quinte?

The question appears
to toe what part of the other specific items of current indebtedness represents loss on operations. I do not think there would be any possibility of giving a definite answer to that.
The Bay of Quinte one does.

I do not think it is correct that the $173,114.58 is the aggregate of loss on operation. I heard it stated and heard the House called upon to leave the Bay of Quinte road out altogether. I do not think that the member for Pictou would be in favour of having a balloon trip over part of the line from here to Toronto. The Bay of Quinte line represents about twenty-nine miles of the Canadian Northern Railway main line between here and Toronto, so if we lift it out we would require an aeroplane line for that twenty-nine miles. That is the value of the suggestion.
The point of the hon. member for Calgary was that that was indebtedness.

There is no doubt that there was a deficit on the Bay of Quinte road operated as an individual road and not connected. How could it be expected to succeed without being connected up and made a portion of a through line? It can be expected to succeed a great deal better when it becomes a part of a system and so gets the benefit of its proportion of a long haul instead of only a short haul. But the facts are these. The company, in acquiring the Bay of Quinte road, acquired the road and the stock at very little more than it would have cost to have built the twenty-eight and a fraction miles of that road which is now comprised in the Canadian Northern Railway line between here and Toronto; and in addition to that it secured about twenty-nine miles more running south to Deseronto, Sydenham and two or three other towns, so by this process and by standing this deficit for a few years, they have 'been able to get access to several good towns and to get practically twenty-nine miles of railway for nothing.
How do you get the one and a quarter millions in the Canadian Northern Railway Quebec?

The Canadian Northern Railway Quebec is in much the same position. It has not 'been paying as an individual line and never was expected to pay. The purpose of the whole uniting up of the system is to make these roads pay as a system. Whether or not the one and a quarter million dollars which appear here as floating indebtedness arise in whole or in part, and of course it does arise in part, from the fact that there is a deficit in operation, the fact is that the road owes that money as current indebtedness and that debt we must assume.

Reverting to the
original question, the sum total is that the banks have in their possession $24,324,000 of securities against which there has been advanced $20,303,000. That is the banks; have a margin of $3,000,000 over and above the loans which have been made. That is what the Premier calls a contingent liability which the Government may ask Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann to see carried through. The liability cannot be a very serious one for the reason that it seems\ to be conceded that the banks in this country, for the last two or three years, have been pursuing a very conservative policy with regard to loans and have a margin of $3,000,000 on the advances which they have made in respect to those securities. Bo that so far as asking Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann individually to assume any contingent liability with regard to that bank debt, I should answer that no one who takes an optimistic view of the condition or has any hope that this enterprise will eventually go through, would say that we are asking Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann to assume anything very serious in the way of a liability, as the banks are already fully secured for that debt. 1 understood the hon. gentleman to say that there are equipment bonds which have been paid out of current revenues of the Canadian Northern railway. If that is so, it is only a question of their being able to sell these equipment bonds and out of the proceeds recoup the Canadian Northern Railway treasury and so reduce the indebtedness down to a normal amount.

The rolling stock company sells the equipment bonds and pays for the equipment outright. All the Canadian Northern railway does is to agree to pay them. They cannot, by selling new bonds, recoup themselves for that amount.
Where is the $6,000,000 to come from? Is there any security against it Out of which the railway company can realize?

No, as I understand
the floating indebtedness must be reduced out of current revenue and it may be-although here I speak with some hesitation- that the amount paid on capital will be recouped from the capital fund and in that way the indebtedness will be reduced, although I cannot speak positively.

What I would apprehend in regard to this discussion is that the revenues of the Canadian Northern railway were used to take up the equipment company bonds in order to find the money to pay the equipment men who are providing the goods, and that they were held in such a way that the Canadian Northern railway, upon a proper market, would be able to have these disposed of and to re-,' coup themselves until such time as the matter could be worked out under the usual provisions of an equipment trust. Is that not the position?

Not as I understand it. What I have understood and what I intended to convey to the House is that annual payments on equipment trusts fell due and the company had; to make these annual payments. As a consequence of making these annual payments on equipment trust bonds, the floating indebtedness rose. There were no other sources from which to make the payment. Whatever the money was paid from it had the effect of raising the floating indebtedness of the company.
In other words, thej revenue of the company was devoted to a greater degree than it should have been in particular years to paying off equipment bonds.
That is exactly it.

Then naturally 1
assume that we ought to look for morei equipment than is included in this security, and I apprehend from what my hon. friend has said that he has no particular data to give us as to the amount of equipment that goes with the roadbed and the franchises and the right of the different companies in addition to that. I wanted to get clear exactly where this alleged liability of Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann was to be asserted on the part of the Govern-268	; .jJt/'lP

ment. I have pointed out that this asking them to assume a sort of collateral security) to the $20,000,000 owing to the banks is not a very onerous proposition; the liability is one which is more imaginary than real, because, the banks have taken good care to see that they are amply secured. It is unfortunate for the purpose of enabling us to ascertain the real value of this security that we have not been furnished with the information we asked for last week as to the assets of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited. We should have such a statement as being very material to the consideration of the value of this security. My right hon. friend says:	These people
owe, under the conditions we have just been discussing, $10,000,000 for equipment and other items. That must be reduced to $3,000,000. The joint stock company of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, have undertaken that they will give covenants and undertakings that that $7,000,000 reduction will be paid. If Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, have a large amount of assets which can be readily liquidated, of course their guarantee will be very substantial and I apprehend that that condition must exist because they are being put forward all through this proposition from beginning to end as being the responsible people; and it is only in the event of the joint stock company of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, not being able to give guarantees which are satisfactory to the Government or in the event of that company not having assets which can be liquidated in order to bring down the indebtedness that the Prime Minister will ask for a guarantee from Mackenzie and Mann individually. That seems to be the situation in which we stand. .

When my hon. friend
from Pictou was asking the Solicitor General some questions about that $6,000,000, my hon. friend stated that his understanding was that that amount was created largely by the payment of equipment bonds as they matured, which means, I suppose, that these bonds are redeemed so many each year. As I understand it, Mackenzie and Mann not having the necessary funds to pay these bonds as they came due took the ordinary money in their possession to meet them and so got into debt. My hon. friend from Pictou has asked the Solicitor General whether there was any security out of which they could be recouped. I understand of course that they could not sell those bonds over again because they have been already

taken up. My hon. friend the Solicitor General says that they may be recouped out of capital. Would my hon. friend explain what that means. The $100,000,000 of stock is all paid up; $60,000,000 goes to Mackenzie, Mann, and Company7, Limited, .and $40,000,000 to the Government, and I do not see any capital in sight except the $45,000,000^which we are now guaranteeing. Did my hon. friend mean to infer that the $6,000,000 might be paid out of the guarantee now before the House. If not, where are the fund® coming from? Perhaps he did not mean to convey that impression.

I certainly did not. I do not think they can in any way be recouped out of the funds now provided. The point I intended to make was this, and no more: that the equipment bonds falling due each month faster than the equipment depreciated brought upon Mackenzie and Mann an extraordinary drain in the way of providing for those equipment trusts, and in that way added to their floating indebtedness. I do not know at the present time that there is any method of reducing that other than out of the revenues of the company, which they have every reason to believe will be increased with the linking up of the system; but if I can explain more fully later on, I will be glad to do so.

That seems to be a fair answer. What has been bothering us on this side of the House is where the money is to come from to pay this $8,000,000. My hon. friend says that as far as the $6,500,000 is concerned, it is largely for the redemption of equipment trust bonds, and he does not see any way of recouping unless somebody digs down into his pocket.
Mr. MEIGHEN; Except out of revenue, which there is every anticipation will increase.

My hon. friend has great faith in believing that they will be able to pay the $6,500,000 out of revenue. That brings me down to another question. I was not here on Wednesday last, and if I ask any questions that have already been answered my hon. friend need not cover the ground again, as I shall be able to look them up in ' Hansard.' I want to refer now to the $16,000,000 odd of equipment bonds mentioned on page 10 of the blue-book. Does that mean that the $16,000,000 has been created by reason of the fact that they have been taking up equipment bonds faster than the rolling stock has depreciated, and that they now

intend to issue new bonds on the partly worn out rolling stock?

The $16,000,000 on
page 10 represents equipment bonds that are still issuable and out of which these moneys will be obtained.
That is, there is equipment in existence against which these bonds may be issued?
Yes. It is put in this column because the $27,441,086 of equipment required to complete is put in the other column.

That is, they expect to buy more equipment and issue bonds against it. As I understand it, there are $7,000,000 of debt due on rolling stock. They are going to buy $20,000,000 of new rolling stock, and against that issue $16,000,000 of equipment bonds. Am I right in assuming that my hon. friend does not include any equity which might now exist by reason of the fact that the rolling stock has not depreciated as rapidly as it has been paid for ?

I cannot answer the latter part of my hon. friend's question, because I did not catch it, but in regard to the first part I may say that the method adopted is to pay twenty-five per cent cash on rolling stock. The company requires $20,000,000 of rolling stock, which is included in the $27,441,086 in the anticipated requirements to complete, on page 10. As against that $20,000,000 there is $16,496,332 of equipment bonds still issuable.
Have they new stock there to represent it ?

About seventy-five per cent. They require about $20,000,000 of rolling stock and they have to pay twenty-five per cent cash and issue equipment bonds for the balance. The $20,000,000 is what they require, and against that they will have the proceeds of $16,496,332 equipment bonds. It is simply a matter of bookkeeping, and the result is that they require in cash the difference between $16,000,000 and $20,000,000, which is what the statement shows.
One more question along that line. I have not the item before me, but I noticed somewhere that there was a debt of $7,000,000 on equipment. Am I right?
The items are given.

I recollect very well that there is $7,000,000 owing on equipment and

they want $20,000,000 more for new equipment. My hon. friend says they have to pay twenty-five per cent of that in cash. That will be about $5,000,000 down. Do I understand that that $5,000,000 as well as the $7,000,000 of debt comes out of the $45,000,000 now being guaranteed ?

They will both come
out of the $100,000,000 that will be available when this guarantee is given.
My hon. friend is hardly explicit enough. Will it come out of the $45,000,000 guarantee?

It cannot be said that it will come out of one or the other, but it will come out Ojf the funds raised by the two together. It will come out of the $100,000,000 and it is immaterial whether it comes out of the $58,000,000 or the $42,000,000.

I would like to have an answer because I am afraid that if the liabilities go on piling up .so fast this $45,000,000 will all be used and they will be wanting another $45,000,000. It is admitted that $21,000,000 has to be paid. That is set out on page 42. That surely has to be paid out of the $45,000,000. Then there is $7,000,000 to be paid to liquidate debts due on equipment. That makes $28,000,000 or practically $29,000,000. If you add to that $5,000,000 more, as cash down on the new rolling stock, it is getting pretty near to the $45,000,000, and I would like to know what they are going to complete the road with.

In addition to the $45,000,000, there is $58,000,000. If the hon. gentleman will look at page 10 of the blue-book he will see that the $100,000,000 is made up of various items spread over six different headings. That $100,000,000 includes the $21,262,527.26. Against that we have the $58,000,000 and we will have the proceeds of the $45,000,000 of securities now being guaranteed which will make up the $100,000,000. There is no apportionment between the $45,000,000 and the $58,000,000 at present. The money has to be expended for the purposes set out in the photograph copies that are on the table.

I have not had the opportunity of discussing this matter with the owners to the extent my hon. friend has. Perhaps my head is a little dense, but I 2684
cannot see where the urgent money is coming from. Figure it out. There is $21,000,000	to	be	paid	at once;$7,000,000	is	due	on	equipment.
To complete the road you have to take $23,000,000 for the Canadian Northern Pacific end of it. I only see $10,000,000 or $11,000 -000 here and that makes about $12,000,000 more than you need on the Pacific end,-: $35,000,000 plus $12,000,000 makes $43,000,000; For the Canadian Northern main line you need $15,000,000, and I see only $7,000,000 against that. That is $7,000,000 more. Your $45,000,000 is gone and you want $15,000,000 besides that.
Page 10 will show it.

I have page 10 before
me. It appears to me that the Canadian Northern will not have money enough this year, although in the future it may be worked out. It seems to me that there is at least $50,000,000 or $55,000,000 required immediately in order to pay these debts, to pay for equipment over and above the securities issuable and to complete the road and they have not the money to do that with. I cannot see more than $41,000 -000 or $42,000,000 with which to meet obligations amounting to $55,000,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If my hon. friend will look at page 10 he will see that the items to which he alluded are included in the sum of $27,441,086. That includes rolling stock to the amount of about $20,000,000 and an amount still to be paid for rolling stock already .acquired. My hon. friend will bear in mind that the amount of $21,252,577.26, set forth on page 42, being the total of accounts outstanding on construction, is included in the $100,000,000 estimated as necessary to complete the road. When all this is taken into account it is misleading to add the $21,000,000 to the $100,000,000. It is included in. the larger amount. We tried to make a very careful investigation for the purpose of .ascertaining whether or not the securities now proposed to be issued will complete the road. The investigation which we have made satisfies us that they will be quite ample for that purpose.

May I ask the Solicitor General to look at page 34. There I find a table showing capital stock authorized and issued from which the following appears :

Canadian Northern railway:
Authorized	$92,900,000
Issued	 77,000,000
Held by Mackenzie, Mann and
Company and associates		70,000,000
May I ask who Mackenzie, Mann and Company and associates are?

I believe the whole
$70,000,000 is in the name of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited. I presume it is put down there as being held by Mackenzie, Mann and Company and associates for the reason that it is likely that it appears in that way in the books of the company. I cannot say who the associates are but, if I may venture a reason, it is that Mackenzie, Mann and Company may Slave understandings with others that in certain events they are to receive a portion of this stock for services rendered. I am sight in saying that the whole of the stock is in the name of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited.

The Minister of Finance stated last year that he had heard of several shares of the stock of the Canadian Northern Railway Company that had been disposed of. I think he referred to the price. That will indicate that there must be some outstanding stock in the hands of some persons other than Mackenzie, Mann and Company. It is generally understood that a certain portion of this stock is held by outside parties. Has the Solicitor General looked into the stock book to ascertain how the stock appears?

Yes, it has been investigated by the auditors and it has been found that $70,000,000 of the stock stands in the name of Mackenzie, Mann and Company. I do not remember the Minister of Finance making the statement which the hon. gentleman alluded to but, if so, it likely arose in this way, that a former manager procured a certain part of the stock as part remuneration and sold it but it has been purchased back since.

Has the Solicitor
(General looked into the question as regards -the value of the subsidiary companies, when they were purchased, how much wa3 paid for them by Mackenzie, Mann and Company, whether stock in these subsidiary (companies is held in the name of a joint stock company or of an individual, or *whether or not the funds necessary to purchase control of a great many of these subsidiary companies came out of the moneys that were earned by way of profit in the
JMr. Pardee. 1
construction of other roads? What information has the Solicitor General about that?

The stocks appearing,
first, as being held by or in trust for the Canadian Northern railway and, next, as being held by Mackenzie, Mann and Company and associates, are held by Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited. That applies to both columns on page 34 in toto. The next part of my hon. friend's question is: Where did they get the money to get hold of the stock of the subsidiary companies? Well, I can answer that, first of all, by saying that none of the money came out of the Canadian Northern railway. In the next place it was not, for the most part, money that secured control. For example, Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, financed the construction of the Canadian Northern Ontario. They undertook the financing required and they gave their services as construction experts to the road and they took the stock of the road for it the same as any one else would do and the same as has been done in many instances that my hon. friends are familiar with. I do not know who else would be entitled to the stock. In the case of the Halifax and Southwestern, there is $1,000,000 of stock and that $1,000,000 of stock came to Mackenzie, Mann and Company by arrangement with the present Government of Nova Scotia. Mackenzie, Mann and Company, in 1902, entered into an arrangement to build railways in Nova Scotia on the basis of twelve and one-half per cent of profit on the expenditure, which is the general rate. The roads were built and Mackenzie, Mann and Company built them on this basis. The Halifax and Southwestern was incorporated and a settlement was made with the Nova Scotia Government a year or two ago, whereby, instead of getting twelve and one-half per cent in lieu of expenditures they had made in acquiring and building these roads, a general settlement was arrived at whereby they took $1,000,030 of stock in the Halifax and Southwestern. The explanation that I have given in regard to the Canadian Northern Ontario applies in the main throughout. We have traced individual subsidiary companies in order to see that the Canadian Northern did not pay moneys out by way of profit to Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, and we find that they did not.
What about the Canadian Northern Saskatchewan?

I see there is a million dollars' worth of stock held in the Canadian Northern Saskatchewan. I have no special information as regards that railway. I presume that they have been allotted the stock by the directors of the company, in lieu of their expenditures.

If what my hon. friend says is correct, namely, that this is stock given to Mackenzie, Mann and Company, in satisfaction of their services in financing these various roads, how does it come that on page 34 of the blue-book submitted for the information of the House, this stock is alleged to be held in trust for the Canadian Northern? If it belongs to Mackenzie, Mann and Company, having been received by them for their services, and if they have got nothing else for their services, how is it held in trust for the Canadian Northern?
Take the Canadian Northern Alberta, authorized stock, $3,000,000; issued, $3,000,000; $3,000,000 held by or in trust for the Canadian Northern railway, or for Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited. Take the Canadian Northwestern railway, authorized stock, $6,000,000; issued, $2,000,000; $2,000,000 held in trust for the Canadian Northern railway. Take the Canadian Northern Saskatchewan, authorized stock, $5,000,000; issued, $1,000,000;	$1,000,000
held in trust for the Canadian Northern railway. Take the Canadian Northern Pacific, the stock issue of which is $25,000,000, which is all alleged here to be held in trust for the Canadian Northern railway. Take the Duluth, Winnipeg and Pacific railway, the stock issue of which is $6,000,000. Of that $3,060,000 is held in trust for the Canadian Northern railway, and $2,940,000 is held by Mackenzie, Mann and Company and associates. Take the Canadian Northern Ontario, of which my hon. friend has just said that Mackenzie, Miann and Company, Limited, have given all their services in financing the road and in securing its construction. The total capital issue is $10,000,000, all of which is alleged to be held in trust for the Canadian Northern railway. Take the Halifax and Southwestern railway. The issued capital is $1,000,000, all of which is alleged to be held in trust for the Canadian Northern railway. According to this statement, $45,000,000 of the stock of these subsidiary companies is alleged to belong to the Canadian Northern, not to Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, at all. If that is so, I would like to know how the hon.
gentleman can say that this stock was issued to Mackenzie, Mann and Company in payment for their services in connection with these various companies.

This point has been
raised in the House before, and 5 p.m. it naturally arises toy reason of the headings in this statement. No objection can toe taken at all to the point being raised, nor to any one wfho goes no further than to ask for the information before erecting a- very large fabric of denunciation upon it.
I did not do that.

My reference is not to
the hon. member for St. John. Permit me to say this, that what I said first was correct. The stock is issued to Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, for their services in construction. That in the main applies, although there may have been other things done as well; but in connection with the roads . in respect of which the stock issues said to be held in trust for the Canadian Northern railway, amounting to about $45,000,000 in all, the Canadian Northern Railway Company has itself rendered services in the way of guarantee of *bonds. Take, for example, the Halifax and Southwestern railway. The Canadian Northern Railway Company has guaranteed its bonds. Take the Canadian Northern Ontario. The Canadian Northern Railway Company has stood between the Government of Canada and loss in that respect. The same applies to the Canadian Northern Pacific. I have a list here and would read it through, if it were necessary; but whenever the Canadian Northern Railway Company itself came in and interested itself in a road, then the stock passed into a mother column, and the trusteeship only goes to this extent that it binds Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, who are still the beneficial owners, not to divert those stocks elsewhere, but to take in lieu of them stock in the Canadian Northern Railway Company. Wherever that connection has arisen up to date between the Canadian Northern Railway Company and the subsidiary companies, then the stock appears to toe held untrammelled in the list of stocks owned by Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, but if the Canadian Northern Railway Company has interposed with its security or guarantee in any way, then the stocks are put in another column and, for convenience only, it is headed 'held in trust'. There is no specific declaration of trust. The stocks

are simply placed there on the tacit understanding that Mackenzie, Mann and Company will take in lieu of them stock in the Canadian Northern Railway Company.
With regard to the Canadian Northwestern Railway Company, those securities are guaranteed by the Alberta Government?
That is correct, but there are other securities not guaranteed.
In addition to the bonds of the Canadian Northwestern railway guaranteed by the Government of Alberta, are there any other outstanding securities which are guaranteed by the Canadian Northern?
My information is that there are, but I cannot give the exact amount. That would be why the stock was placed in this column instead of in the other.
I would like to get that amount.
I will try to get it.

The same with the
Canadian Northern Alberta. Take the Canadian Northern Pacific railway. I understand the British. Columbia Government guaranteed their bonds to the enormous sum of $45,000 a mile. In addition to those bonds guaranteed by the province, are there any other securities of the Canadian Northern Pacific which are guaranteed independently of the Government by the Canadian Northern, and what are they?

In the first place, the hon. gentleman must remember that, even though the securities are guaranteed by the Alberta Government and by the British Columbia Government respectively, the Canadian Northern Railway Company in each case guarantees the Alberta Government and the British Columbia Government against loss, and in that way renders service in relation to these roads, and in that way justifies their being placed in the agreement as being held in trust. So far as the second part of my hon. friend's observations are concerned, if the hon. gentleman will look at numbers 21 and 22 of what I call the key statement, at page 30 of the blue book, he will see the division there. 41 per cent debenture stock (Alberta)-that means guaranteed by Alberta -$6,424,000. 4 per cent .bonds not guaranteed by Alberta, $2,800,000. That, I

believe, is the correct division. That, at all events, is what appears on the auditors' statement.
Will the Government recognize the guarantees made by the Canadian Government as a liability against the Canadian Northern prior to the lien for the $45,000,000 now asked to be guaranteed?
Has the hon. gentleman reference to the guarantee on the Canadian Northern Ontario?

Take the case of the
Halifax and Southwestern-there the liability is guaranteed to the Government of Nova Scotia by the Canadian Northern railway, I understand. Will the Government recognize that guarantee as a lien on the Canadian Northern railway as preceding the one which the Government will acquire by virtue of the proposed guarantee?

I do not understand
that the Canadian Northern railway guarantees in that case, or in any other so far as I recall, has the effect of making a lien on this road; it is simply the individual guarantee of the company.

Unless the knowledge
the Government now have of that lien might have some legal effect upon their position as a later creditor, as it were. I merely wanted to know how the Government looked at it.

On page 30 there is the list of securities issued by these different companies and totalling $312,000,000. On page 45 there is .a list of a total of $24,000,000 of securities of the Canadian Northern railway and allied companies pledged. Is this amount of $24,000,000 in addition to the $312,000,000?

The smaller amount is included in the larger. I was going to amplify my statement to the hon. member for Carleton, N.B. The discussion may possibly have led to the idea that the $24,000,000 of securities was in addition to the $312,000,000, but that is not the case.
These are simply collateral and represent no indebtedness beyond the $312,000,000.

In regard to the
issuing of contemplated securities generally for the Government, $45,000,000, apparently there are other securities to the amount of $58,000,000 referred to at page 10, forming the credit side of the account of the financing of the road. Has the Government entered into any understanding with the Canadian Northern Kailway Company by which these two lots of securities are 'to be financed together, or is it the intention of the Government to handle the financing of the $45,000,000 alone?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It will be observed that
the $58,000,000 is made up in part of subsidies which will be available as soon as they are earned. So far as the proceeds of the securities sold are concerned they also are eliminated. So far as the rolling stock is concerned, the hon. gentleman understands that has not yet been issued.
But do I understand that these securities for $58,000,000 on the credit side of the account have been disposed of?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Sonne of them have been disposed of and the proceeds are available as soon as they are earned, like the subsidies. The hon. gentleman will observe that this list is not made up altogether of securities but in part of subsidies. The first item of $6,704,097 is 'Canadian Northern Pacific Railway 44 per cent Debenture Stock and Subsidy.' Then the third item ' Canadian Northern Ontario Railway; proceeds of securities in hand and subsidy to be earned, $16,788,822.' The ' Canadian Northern, Pacific new securities, $4,854,500 ' have not been sold according to the latest information I have. I think that in all cases these are placed at the realised or realizable amount.

Will the securities
to be guaranteed be disposed of by this Government or by the company?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The securities are disposed of in such cases with the approval of the Government by arrangement with the Minister of Finance. The trust deed in such cases makes express provision.
The hon. gentleman's question is: has the money been raised to the full face value of the note?
Yes, and the money expended?

All except the charges has been raised. It does not follow that it has been spent, nor does it follow that it is in the hands of the railway company to spend. It is in the hands of the Receiver General or treasurer of the province, because against that guaranteed bonds of Albeiita have been placed; The money will be in the hands of the treasurer of the province of Alberta, and can only^ earned in accordance with the provisions of their statute.

That is what I want to vet at, but I want to get at it a little more definitely. If the amount stated to have been raised on the secured gold note is money for expenditure, why is it raised on the secured note instead of on the sale of the bonds?

There are two reasons. In the first place, the time might be inopportune for the sale of the bonds, and so it pays the company to raise the money temporarily on notes, placing the bonds as security, and as the market grows more favourable they make the sale outright and recoup the holder of the notes. Another reason is that the company may not need all the money at once, and it pays it better to issue notes for a part and place a part of the guaranteed bonds as collateral. Both reasons apply.

Does my hon. friend think that if the company raises only a part of the money that can be raised out of these guarantee bonds, that money is placed to the credit of the provincial treasurer and paid out only on the authority of the provincial treasurer?
Yes, that is the fact.
My impression would be that under this system of finance the necessity of complying with that condition might be avoided.
The auditors check the balance to the credit of the provincial treasurer in each ease and ascertain that there has 'been no deviation from the terms of the statute in that regard.
The terms of the statute do not contemplate a transaction of this character.

I think so. It may not do so in so many words, but the moment you pledge the bonds guaranteed by the Al'berta Government, the terms of the statute apply to anything and everything raised by that pledge.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I know that is the case so far as this Government is concerned, because I had occasion to make direct inquiry from the Minister of Finance, and was informed by him that bonds guaranteed by this Government may be used by way of pledge only with the consent of the Government and the money must be deposited to the credit of the Minister of Finance or the Receiver General.

I find on pages 30, 31, 32 and 33 of the blue-book the par value of the securities and also the proceeds and the actual withdrawals. On page 33, the actual withdrawals from the proceeds of the securities mentioned on pages 30-33 are set down at $217,729,310.35. Of these total withdrawals the amount used on construction is $164,422,303.78, leaving a balance of other withdrawals, $52,617,006.57. Has my hon. friend a statement-I do not mean in detail, but under different heads- of what that $52,000,000 was withdrawn for?
The details, of course, are given in the statement, but it does not show just where the money went.
It seems a good deal of money to~ be used outside of construction.i

The facts are these.
The $164,422,303.78 under the head 'withdrawals on construction1 represents the amount withdrawn from the proceeds of securities and used by Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, on construction. The total amount that passed through the books of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, arising out of the proceeds of securities is $164,422,303.78. The remainder, $52,617,006.57, represents the proceeds of se-

curities used on construction but not used through Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, the construction department of the Canadian Northern. The method is this: Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, do the construction proper, but after the road is in a position to be taken off the hands of the contractors there is a great deal of work still to be done and that is done by the Canadian Northern direct, not through the construction department, and is done usually after the road is being oper-* ated. This $52,000,000 is comprised largely of betterments. It represents the whole amount of the proceeds of securities that have been applied to the road, but not through Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited. The details are given on page 29 of the blue-book, where the hon. gentleman will see that the total amount expended is not $52,617,006.57, but $61,183,662.82. According to 'the details given on page 29, this money was applied to reduction of equipment trusts, direct purchase of equipment, direct purchase of equipment for allied lines, betterments, acquired securities, advance to railway companies allied to the Canadian Northern railway, and so on, making a total of $61,183,662.82. But that $61,000,000 is comprised not only of the proceeds of securities, but also of other moneys that were similarly expended and which arose not from securities but from land funds and sundry accounts. Reference to the other side of the ta,ble shows that the $52,000,000 is made up of the $48,815,516.92, proceeds of unguaranteed securities and $3,801,489.65, proceeds of guaranteed securities. These are the moneys expended by the Canadian Northern for the purposes set out under expenditure on page 29.
I understand, then, that the $52,000,000 mentioned on page 32, together with other withdrawals, is included [DOT] in and forms part of the $61,000,000 on page 29?

And comprises the
first two items for the proceeds of securities as distinguished from the proceeds of land funds and sundry accounts.

When the contract
was let to the Mackenzie and Mann Construction Company by the Canadian Northern railway, were tenders called for and was the contract awarded to the lowest tenderer?

The hon. gentleman is under a misapprehension if he assumes that the contracts were let to Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited. The contracts were not let to Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited; Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, simply acted for the Canadian Northern and let contracts themselves. They simply acted, as I have very often said, as the construction department. Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, where they found that it could be done advantageously, did advertise for tenders. Particularly did they do so in connection with the very piece of line in respect of \hich an engineer wrote to an hon. member of this House saying that if they had advertised they could have built the line at 40 per cent less. Tenders were asked for and many tenders were received for that piece of line.
What is the name of the company that h^s done most of the construction work?

I could not say as to
most of the construction work; I presume my hon. friend is right when he implies that one company did most of the work. The name is the Northern Construction Company, Limited.
Who is the president of that company?

I do not know who the president is, but I do know from the investigation we have made that neither Sir William Mackenzie nor Sir Donald Mann or any one interested in the Canadian Northern has any interest whatever in that company.
The Prime Minister filed an affidavit showing who were the officers of this construction company, from which it appears that neither Sir William Mackenzie nor Sir Donald Mann is directly interested.
Would the hon. gentleman inform us who the members of the company are ?

I have forgotten the
names of the parties, but I remember the Prime Minister filing that paper.
I have an impression that a Mr. Mackenzie is the general manager of the Northern Construction Company.
But he is no relation of Sir William, according to the affidavit.
Is the hon. gentleman quite sure ?
Who made the affidavit ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is made by three men: the president, the vice-president, and a director.
Were the affidavits filed here sworn before Mr. Z. A. Lash ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.

In the East an affidavit sworn before a person as directly interested as Mr. Lash is in this affair would not be accepted in any court of law; but possibly this high court of Parliament is not hound by the rules applied to other courts.
In a non-contentious matter in Ontario an affidavit taken in that way would be accepted.
If the hon. gentleman will read down the same column he will see.
Do the five items following apply to this ?
I suppose these are short term notes.
There is a table filed showing when they mature. These are short-term notes, some six months, some a year, some more.

We will assume that money has been raised to the face value of the notes and has been expended, and the notes become due and the market conditions are still as they were, or worse; what happens then ?

There would be several courses. The note might be renewed, the mortgage might be taken at whatever it was worth and the proceeds sold, or they might raise on other notes the amount required to retire these two notes.

Suppose that the worst
should happen and that these debentures would have to be forced on the market and sold at a sacrifice; they would not realize

the amount for which they were collateral. Who suffers in that case?

When the collaterals
are pledged they are pledged on certain specific terms giving power of sale to the pledgee, and to those terms the Government interested must be a party. If these have been pledged the Government of Alberta must have been a party to the terms of the pledge, and although the market may fall, although there may be a sacrifice, the Government of Alberta has been a consenting party to that eventuality. The loss of course, will fall on the railroad. The proceeds would be just that much less.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Whoever borrowed the
money would be liable for the balance.

That is what I am trying to get at. If the railway company borrows the money on the guarantee of the province would the province have to implement the guarantee or has the province no interest in the matter beyond the guarantee?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It has an interest in seeing that as large an amount is secured as possible from the loans guaranteed by it. The securities would be sold, they would stand as securities for which the credit of the province was pledged. The province would have to meet them when they fell due in the future. But ,if the securities were not sold for a sufficient amount to meet the debt for which they were pledged, then the lender of the money, the holder of the securities, would have a legitimate claim against persons or corporations who effected the loan for any balance that might still remain due.
That would be a contract between the Tailway company that borrowed the money and the lenders of the money. Supposing the money had been expended, the province would have already received the benefit.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The province would not
lose anything directly. It would indirectly lose in this way, that the railway companies, having less money available for the purpose of carrying out the enterprise, would not be in as good a position to proceed with it.

My hon. friend from
Toronto (Mr. Bristol) was good enough to send to me the ' Hansard ' of May 13, in which there is an affidavit stating that

the officers of the Northern Construction Company are A. R. Mann, Archibald Mackenzie and C. 'Cummings. My hon. friend *was of the impression, and so stated to the committee, that that affidavit showed that the shareholders of the Northern Construction Company, which I understand did most of the construction work under Mackenzie, Manni and Company, Limited, -were in no way related to Mackenzie, Mann and Company. My hon. friend said that the affidavit showed that. I have read the affidavit carefully but it states no such thing. What it says is this:
We, Alexander Robert Mann, of the city of Vancouver, in the province of British Columbia, and Archibald Mackenzie, and Charles Cummings, both of the city of Winnipeg, in the province of Manitoba, do and each of us doth hereby declare :
1.	That we are President, Vice-President and Secretary-Treasurer respectively of the Northern Construction Company, Limited.
2.	That we have a full knowledge of all the affairs of said company. [DOT]
3.	That neither1 Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, nor any shareholder or director in such company, nor Sir William Mackenzie, nor Sir Donald Mann, have any interest of any kind whatsoever, directly or indirectly, in the Northern Construction Company, Limited, or in its capital stock, or in its property or assets of any description, or in any profits or earnings resulting from the company's operations, contracts, or works.
But it does not state that they are in no way related to Sir William Mackenzie or Sir Donald Mann.

My point was that
neither Sir William Mackenzie nor Sir Donald Mann were directly or indirectly connected with the Northern Construction Company. I have heard from another source that Sir William Mackenzie is in no way related, to the Archibald Mackenzie of the Northern Construction Company. I believe, however, that Sir Donald Mann is a brother of Alexander Mann mentioned in the affidavit.
My hon. friend stated that the affidavit showed that they were in no way related.
I did not mean to say that; what I meant to say was that Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann were not connected either directly or indirectly with the Northern Construction Company.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am informed that the Mr. MacKenzie mentioned in the affidavit is in no way related to Sir William

Mackenzie, bu>t that the Alexander Mann is a brother of Sir Donald Mann.

This section says:
Grant a specific mortgage or charge upon the mortgage securities and shares of stock now or from time to time hereafter deposited with and specifically mortgaged under the trust deed of the 30th day of June, 1903.
Is that the deed under which the convertible stock was created?

No, this refers to the
4 per cent perpetual.
Is not this the deed which gives the holders the right to exchange convertible for common stock?
My recollection is that the date of that deed is 1910.
The point I want to make is this: This does not permit the creation of any securities which become convertible so as to increase the common stock?
No.

Clause agreed to.
On clause e: ' New Trust Deed' to
Grant fixed, specific and floating mortgages or charges upon the undertaking of the Canadian Northern and its properties, assets, rents and revenues, and its rights, powers and franchises, present and future.

I would like the
Solicitor General to state how much of equipment there is to which the mortgage will attach, and how- that mortgage will stand as regard priority.

I asked before dinner
that a table be provided showing the value of the equipment that was clear from encumbrances; tha't is, what equipment trusts had been paid off. That will require a collection to be made from a very large number of papers, but I will present it to the House as soon as ready. I have been informed that the information I gave the House this morning is correct, that there was a considerable amount of equipment clear of encumbrances, not only equipment purchased direct but also through equipment trusts. This clause will have the effect of giving the Government security against an equity of about $27,000,000 in the equipment already purchased under equipment trusts. That is the amount that has been paid off and the equity would be that amount less depreciation.
What would be the depreciation?

My information is that they have been keeping up their depreciation and that the equity in the equipment would represent practically the whole $27,000,000. The company's own car works are for the purpose of preventing depreciation as far as possible.

I cannot believe my hon. friend to be sincere in saying that there would be no depreciation in the rolling stock of the company, because all he has to do is to travel along the right of way of any road and see the cars that are switched off on the sidings and which have practically become useless. There must certainly be depreciation in that case.
These are replaced by other cars that are not charged to capital but to revenue.

If that be so, they would probably be able to keep them up. Now, I want to know whether any statement has been given to the committee showing what mortgages or liabilities exist prior to the mortgage which is going to be given as provided for by subsection 3 of this clause. We might work it out. We know that the Dominion Government have a mortgage on the Canadian Northern Ontario, which, I believe, is a first mortgage. Then we have some sort of a security on the remainder of the Canadian Northern system. British Columbia has a first mortgage upon the British Columbia end, and the same would be true of the different provinces. I would like the hon. gentleman to state in a concise form the exact liabilities that exist prior to the mortgage we are taking. I understand from the discussion that in some cases this would be a fourth mortgage, and I am of opinion that it would, in some other cases, be a fifth mortgage.

I cannot in any way amplify the statement that appears on page 30 of the blue-book. That gives all the charges against the Canadian Northern railway, bu/t of course it cannot be held that the Canadian Northern is alone liable for all of these eighteen charges that appear there. There are many charges there that are on other properties; for instance, the land charge. The notes, of course, cannot be said to be a separate charge. They are the instruments that represent the loan. We can eliminate the notes, the land, the equipment, and the terminals and the rest of the eighteen items appearing on page 30 would be charges

against the road. The income bonds are not charges against the road except to the extent to which the income may be earned. If there is no dividend declared, then they cannot get a dividend and they have no claim against the road.
My hon. friend has hardly caught the idea that I have. On pages 30, 32 and 33 we have a statement to the effect that there are outstanding charges of $312,818,910.42.
I do not mean all the items, but just the first eighteen.
That would be about $193,000,000 of charges which take priority.
Except the notes, the terminals, the land and mortgages on the equipment.
Do we not get a mortgage upon the land subject to whatever liabilities exist upon it at present and also on the terminals?
Yes, but you cannot say that because there is a mortgage on the land it is prior to us as to the railway.
If there is a mortgage upon the land now, it is prior to us.
On the land.

It is prior to us. Anyway, I think I am safe in saying that there are $312,000,000 of securities against this undertaking prior to our $45,000,000 mortgage. I think I am right in making that statement.
Upon the whole undertaking, including all the allied companies the land and equipment, there is a mortgage of $312,000,000.
There are prior mortgages then of $312,000,000 and ours comes in second to them.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, not second to them.

Well, second, or third,
or fourth, or whatever it may be. We come in after these mortgages amounting to $312,000,000. ,
These are not all against the Canadian Northern railway.
I am talking about the undertaking.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Our mortgage is on the
Canadian Northern.
We only get a mortgage on the Canadian Northern. Well, that has mortgages amounting to $193,932,000 against it.
No.

Against the Canadian
Northern property but not all against the Canadian Northern railway itself. Some of it is against land and some against equipment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is all against the Canadian Northern system.

Against the Canadian
Northern and its assets.
Then there will be prior liabilities of about $191,000,000 or $192,000,-000-I make it $193,000,000-against the Canadian Northern and its assets.
And its assets.

And we are coming in
second to that. Could my hon. friend give us a statement showing how the securities prior to our mortgage rank? There would be a first mortgage on the property to the extent of $191,000,000 or $192,000,000 and we would come second or third after that. Of course, it would be interesting if we had a statement setting forth all these securities.

In some cases one mortgage would be first and in other cases an-otaer would be first. On the land there are two land grant mortgages amounting to about $6,000,000 and then a $17,000,000 loan and then we come next as far as the land is concerned..
That would be $23,000,000 -against the land altogether?

Against the land and
townsites leaving us -an equity of about $12,000,000. Then against the equipment we come next after a charge of about $23,000,000. I may not be quite right there. As against the property in Alberta the first charge. would (be $6,776,000 as against the Canadian Northern railway in Alberta. That is not against the Canadian Northern Alberta ibut the Canadian Northern proper in Alberta. Then there would be the perpetual debenture -stock mortgage. I do not think the hon. gentleman himself will have any trouble in taking the papers that are on file and working out these results. Of course, I am quite prepared to 'have it done for him and to show in each ease the order of tire various mortgages. The dates are given in the papers filed.
[Mr. Meighen.l

I would like to have
that and also the due dates of the different securities.
They are already filed. Mr. CARVELL:	In the statement?
There has been a statement prepared and filed of the due dates of the various securities.
If that was included in a statement and put on 'Hansard ' it would 'be very much more valuable.

I have gone through the papers laid on the table of the House, and I do not find that information. I find a statement of which pages 30, 31 and 32 are copies, but I do not find anything in the statement other than what I find in the blue-book. I may have overlooked something. It would be interesting if the House had a tabulated statement showing the priority of these different securities and their due dates, so that we would have some idea of what liabilities this company ie going to be called upon in the future to assume. On this side of the House we are naturally somewhat skeptical and ratheT afraid that the country is going to be called upon to assume very heavy liabilities because of becoming a partner, or a minority stockholder, if my hon. friend likes that term better. Although we are about to become a minority stockholder, we are the only stockholder who has any money, and, when the debt matures, we shall be the people to be called upon to pay it.

If my hon. friend will look at the statement under the heading 'Canadian Northern Railway system, dates of payment, principal and interest'-it may not .appear in the blue-book, but is filed on the table of the House under that heading-he will find every issue, the date of maturity and the date of the payment of the interest.

If you look at page 30 of the blue-book, you will find at least nine items of debenture stocks that have been issued. There are debenture stock items numbers 4, 5, 6, 7 and 9 under provincial guarantees. In regard to tuese securities, I assume that there are trust deeds in existence by which the undertaking of the Canadian Northern in each particular province and all of its assets are mortgaged to secure the guarantee of these -securities by the provincial Government.
The provincial governments, I apprehend, as is usual under these circumstances, retain for themselves the right to control the question of location and various other details in connection with the construction of the road. After we have declared these railways to be for the general advantage of Canada, what is the status of the provinces in this regard? Is the Dominion to recognize their right to control the question of location in regard to the various portions of the road that may not be completed? Each provincial government, having performed its executive and legislative acts within the realm over which it is supreme, has certain rights which permits it to take possession. Having regard to the various provincial mortgages, I ask: Where does the Dominion come in under this assumed declaration that these railways are for the general advantage of Canada?
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) made inquiries regarding the effect of the declaration contained in the fifteenth paragraph of the resolutions? The inquiry, as I understood it, related to railways the construction of which is provided for out of the securities guaranteed by the provinces but to which no portion of the aid provided by these resolutions will be applied. The particular question was as to the routing or location, was it not?

How far would the terms of this agreement interfere with the provisions of trust deeds executed by the provinces relating to portions of this system within those provinces? Would those roads receive aid if this Act went through? I pointed out that we propose to grant a supplementary aid which may conflict with the terms of the provincial arrangements under their several trust deeds. The question is how far this Act would interfere with the jurisdiction of the provincial governments in carrying out the terms of trust deeds guaranteeing securities.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: So far as the disposition of the money is concerned, I understand that we should not interfere with that in the slightest degree; the absolute control remains with the provincial Government.
And the terms of the trust deed would apply?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I understand so. But I will give consideration to the matter and when we come to section 15 I will be prepared to deal with it further if desired.

The reason I asked at this juncture was that we were dealing with a mortgage to be given to the Canadian Northern railway under subsection c, and turning to that I find that there are outstanding debenture stocks which had been issued under security of the guarantee of the Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba governments.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: Are there any charges against these properties except those mentioned in this trust deed?

No, there is no other
charge.

I renew the
observation. I made this morning that the stocks referred to ought to be included in the resolution, for the obvious (reason that if one year or ten years from now anybody turns to the statute he will not find the trust deeds which are made a part of the agreement and which must be referred to in order to understand them. I do not insist upon this to-day, but I think the hon. gentleman should take it into consideration.

I am under the impression now that the trust deed referred to here was set out in .another ratifying statute, in which ease any one would have

easy access to it; if not, the suggestion of my right hon. friend might well be considered.

But even if
it is in another statute, one might be at a loss to find it. One naturally turns to this statute to find what he wants to know.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We will take that into
consideration.

I have not yet 'been able to follow the moneys mentioned in this subsection. For the purpose of my present-inquiry I will not trouble about that. It is agreed that there shall be granted -a specific charge upon the equity of redemption of Mackenzie, Mann, and Company in certain capital stock and debenture stock of the Canadian Northern Town Properties, Limited. Has any means been taken to find out what the equity of redemption in these properties is worth?

Yes, I have stated that to the House. A table is filed giving an estimate and I understand that it is very moderate and below the actual value, and it shows the equity of redemption to be worth between $11,000,000 and $12,000,000.
That is a large amount of money, and I would be much interested in knowing on what basis that estimate is made.

The document filed
shows that.
Has my hon. friend the details with regard to the townsite of War-man, which is an important junction point on the Canadian Northern railway?

No, but I will read a statement in that regard; it is very short. We have not the particulars as to any individual townsite. My hon. friend will note, by reference to the trust deed, that the mere naming of the townsite occupies seven long pages. The land grants and the townsites are in together, and this provision takes the equity that we have in those lands. The statement says that the number of townsites owned in full is 344, 67,500 acres. One-half interest in 172 other towns, total estimated' value $10,500,000. The amount payable in respect of land sold on which instalments are payable within eighteen months is $885,834, and within three years, $2,065,000. The total value, plus the amounts receivable, is $13,450,834. In respect of land grants, the value of unsold

land, over 800,000 acres, is estimated at $12,000,000. The hon. gentleman will ses that this is a very low estimate, because on the 'basis on which lands are selling now, they would be worth considerably more than that. There are 857,000 instead of 800,000 acres so to be valued. There is payable by instalments on lands sold on which at least the first payment has been made, $6,852,445, and there is in the hands of trustees for the payment of prior mortgages and charges, $2,424,451, making a total of $21,276,896. Adding this to the town-sites, we have $34,727,730, against which the total securities amount to $27,288,200, leaving an equity of $11,439,930.

1 would not care to discuss the valuation of what might be called the farm lands, hut in regard to the town-sites it strikes me that there is apt to be a very' serious over-valuation in the statement which has been made. My hon. friend says that the names of the townsites cover six pages. That means, of course, that every station on all the lines of these companies an the four western provinces is a townsite, and the acreage of each townsite would run anywhere from 160 to 640 acres, or perhaps more. Everybody who has had western experience knows that when a railway is built and the townsite is put on the market, what is practically the cream of the townsite is taken then and there and what remains of it is, in 95 cases out of 100, not an asset but a liability. As soon as the town is incorporated, if it is incorporated, at once taxes are levied and the owners of the small acreage that has been sold proceed1 as a matter of religious duty to levy taxes having in view the large acreage that remains unsold. Under the single tax system which very properly prevails in the West, I venture to say that 95 per cent of those townsites that have already been exploited, as, I think under the able and enterprising management of our friend Colonel A. D. Davidson, they have been, is a liability in respect of taxation' and not an asset with regard to sale value. While I do not attach any importance in connection with this agreement to the so-called securities that aTe taken, I merely want to point out what to my mind is ia glaring case in which what is presented to the public as a security is really a liability; it is no security at all. So far as these townsites aTe concerned, the alleged valuation that is given to them is merely an evidence of the vivid' imagination of the talented gentlemen who have to
deal with them and they really should have no standing in the consideration of this measure by Parliament.

The hon. gentleman
will, of course, admit that if we had by any chance left them out of the securities, they would have been very valuable. We did not have a valuation of each townsite made; I do not think it will be suggested that we should have, but by comparing the acreage the hon. gentleman can see that they are taken at an acreage value of $125 an acre, and it will scarcely be suggested that, taken all in all, that is a high valuation.
