I would certainly say that under the present conditions of the real estate market and having in view the fact that all these towns were milked to a finish when they were first established, if they were so established, $150 an acre is a high price for the remainder of the so-called townsite area. I am not saying anything about the exceptional towns; five per cent may have some value, but ninetydive per cent, I would say, is surely a liability, not an asset.

Have the Government had a valuation made of the properties which are to enter into the Canadian Northern system, showing the estimated value per mile, the cost and value of terminals and other equipment, so as to be able to take each system separatively and arrive at some idea of their actual cost and the charges against them?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I understand that the
railway company have made a valuation; I do not think that we made any. Considering the fact that portions of the road were built when labour and material were much cheaper than they are now and that terminals and property of that kind have greatly increased in value, it is thought that the value of the road is very considerably in excess, of the amount that has been expended on it.
The Government are not in a position to submit to the committee any figures showing the estimated value of each system?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not know whether a physical valuation of the whole system would be of any service; at any rate, it would take a very long time to get it.

There is no doubt that a large proportion of the prairie roads represent a very low valuation; it is only reason-

able that they should. A purely branch line, built for purely branch line purposes, cannot be expected to be built and maintained at the high standard of a through line. That must be taken for granted. As a matter of fact a large proportion of their mileage in the West is at a very low physical valuation.

Would the Solicitor
General state if he was in error in stating that the townsites of British Columbia besides Port Mann were included?

No, I cannot state the condition precisely.
Om section 3, subsections a and b:
That before a guarantee is given the following conditions shall be complied with:
(a)	The agreement a draft whereof is set forth in the third schedule hereto (hereinafter called the ' agreement '), shall be duly executed by the parties thereto, and the Governor in Council is hereby authorized to execute the same.
(b)	There shall be transferred to and vested in the trustee as part of the mortgaged premises the shares of stock mentioned in sub-clause (a) of section 2 of these resolutions free from prior charges thereon, such shares to become and to remain the property of the Canadian Northern, subject to the charges created by and to the terms of the new trust deed. Provided that the necessary shares to qualify the directors and preserve the corporate entities of the respective companies may remain in the name of such directors and other necessary parties, but the share certificates ready for transfer shall be delivered to and held by or for the trustee of the new trust deed.

Do I understand that this provision is intended to compel Mackenzie, Mann and Company to transfer over to the Canadian Northern railway all shares of these subsidiary companies that are now held by Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited?
All the shares mentioned in subsection a of section 2; that is, the shares mentioned in the first part of the second schedule.
Would it not be better to amend that clause to read ' such share certificates ' in place of ' these share certificates?'

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The certificates have not been mentioned before.
The shares are mentioned.

We have
reached what I think is a very serious consideration in regard to the stock of

all these companies. The stock of all these companies, according to the blue-book placed before us, is $158,611,000. That is the stock enumerated as issued. Then there is the Canadian Northern Manitoba Railway Company with stock authorized of $1,000,000, which has not yet been issued. There is also the Mount Royal Tunnel and Terminal Company, with $5,000,000 stock * authorized and not yet issued, making a total of $158,000,000. From this is to be deducted $77,000,000, the stock of the parent company, leaving $81,611,000. What becomes of this stock? My hon. friend has just stated that it is handed over to the Canadian Northern railway, who become the owners of it from the passing of this Bill. But that stock is not extinguished. As I understand, the owners of the stock still have power to dispose of it. I cannot understand the resolution otherwise. If I am wrong in this, I would be glad to hear my hon. friend correct me. As I read the resolution, the $81,000,000 stock of the subsidiary companies becomes the property of the parent company, the Canadian Northern railway. This stock, as I understood, was intended to be mobilized in the hands of the Canadian Northern railway and not to be disposed of, that it was tp remain dormant in their hands. I understood the speech of my hon. friend to mean this; but as I read the resolution it certainly conveys to my mind the impression that the stock goes into the hands and possession of the Canadian Northern railway, and can he disposed of by them. The only statement which we have on this is in clause b, which we have just read. The words ' to remain ' are the only words which it seems to me are intended to convey the impression which was given to us by the Solicitor General the other day, that they were to be mobilized in the hands of the Canadian Northern railway and to remain there. If that is the intention, it seems to me that these words are hardly strong enough to make that dis- -position beyond peradventure. Turning to the contract, it seems to confirm my first impression. The contract is in these words-clause 2 paragraph a:
That the contractors will forthwith, upon the execution hereof, transfer or cause to be transferred to the trustee all the shares of capital stock of the constituent and subsidiary companies mentioned in the first and second parts of the schedule hereto, and the said shares'shall form part of the mortgaged premises . . .
The absolute ownership of all the shares mentioned in the first part of the said schedule shall he vested in the Canadian Northern, sub-

ject only to the charge thereon created hy and to the terms of the new trust deed; and the beneficial ownership of all the shares mentioned in the second part of the said schedule shall be vested in the Canadian Northern, subject only to the rights now or hereafter possessed by the National Trust Company, Limited, and the British Empire Trust Company, Limited, under the trust deed of the 80th of June, 1903, securing the perpetual consolidated debenture stock of the Canadian Northern, and to the charge thereon created by and to the terms of the new trust deed.
It seems very plain that the terms of the contract confer on the Canadian Northern the ownership of these shares with only one qualification; that is, the mortgages secured by the trust deed. In other respects their ownership of the shares is unimpaired; they have all the rights of the owner and can sell their equity in the shares to anybody they please. That is one view of the case. Another view is this: This stock ie not in any way extinguished, it remains absolutely as it is. The Canadian Northern will have $100,000,000 of stock of the parent company and they will also be owners of $81,000,000 of the stock of the subsidiary companies. Therefore, the Canadian Northern will have in their own hands $100,000,000 of the stock of the parent company, with the exception of the $40,000,000 that is to be given to Canada and the $81,000,000 of the subsidiary companies, so that there will be against this enterprise $181,000,000 of stock. Suppose the enterprise is profitable, will dividends have to be paid on all this $181,000,000? I understood that the intention of the Government was to limit the stock of the parent and subsidiary companies to $100,000,000, thereby ensuring that dividends would be paid on only $100,000,000 of stockl But, in my judgment, the resolution as framed is susceptible of quite a different interpretation, and it is only fair that we should know exactly what is the intention of the Government and whether they are satisfied with the present drafting of the resolution.	-'~

The first point raised
by the right hon. gentleman is that the clause is not strong enough to prevent the Canadian Northern dealing with these shares. He draws attention to the fact, which is true, that the shares of these subsidiary companies pass into the Canadian Northern impressed only with the charge for the $45,000,000 mortgage. Passing so to the Canadian Northern, they become the property of the Canadian Northern, and 269
being the property of the Canadian Northern, my right hon. friend's argument is that they might transfer them elsewhere, and he doubts whether the words ' and to remain ' will be sufficient td retain the stock in the treasury of the Canadian Northern. I would think that with those word ' and to remain ' in the clause no court could possibly sanction the passing out of the stocks. .'If they pass out they do not remain. But, supposing the words 'and to remain' were not there at all: it would be a practical impossibility for the Canadian Northern ever to dispose of those stocks. Why? They come in impressed as they come with the charge for the $45,000,000 mortgage. That is clear. That is the only thing against them as they reach the treasury of the Canadian Northern, but the moment they become the property of the Canadian Northern, they, like every other portion of its property, become subject to all the charges against the Canadian Northern road. My right hon. friend will readily see that stocks in the treasury of the Canadian Northern, subject first of all to our $45,000,000 mortgage, and then subject to all the other charges against the assets of the Canadian Northern, could never be disposed of by the Canadian Northern.
Legally, but not profitably.

Not practicably. No one would purchase those shares because they would be subject to about $360,000,000 of liabilities; so that even if the words 'and to remain' were not there, I do not think it would be a business possibility for tne Canadian Northern to dispose of the stock. The words are inserted to make it doubly clear that the intention is to compel the rest of those stocks into the treasury of the Canadian Northern as their property. The second point raised by my right hon. friend is that the total of the capitalization of the parent and subsidiary companies is going to be $181,000,000. I take issue with him there. My right hon. friend will remember that, speaking across the floor of the House to myself about four or five days ago, he made the statement that I had assured the House that the stocks of these subsidiary companies were to be wiped out, and that I had made the statement again and again. II did not think that I had been under any obsession when I addressed the House, so I went oveT my speech carefully, and I find that I made no
revised edition

such assertion or anything that could be interpreted as such. I stated very clearly that nobody for a moment suggested that the stocks were to be wiped out in any way. The stocks will exist intact, and the entities of the companies will exist intact when the stock of the subsidiary companies becomes the property of the parent company, just as the railroad of the parent company is its property. The effect of that is to reduce the capitalization that can call for dividends. Hereafter, all the stocks are the property of the parent company whose capitalization is fixed at $100,000,000, and the only person or the only corporation that can come before the Railway Commission or the Government and people of Canada and say: We have a right to dividends, is the Canadian Northern Railway Company. They own everything, and when they come they must say: Our stock is $100,000,000, and no more. Consequently, we have reduced the capitalization to $100,000,000 and only $100,000,000, and not one dollar more, can carry with it the right to call for dividends.

Is there any method by which the Government, if it so desire, can receive representation on the board of directors of any subsidiary company ? The voting power would be with the Canadian Northern, I suppose, because they would have the majority.
If I caught the point rightly, the answer is that we have power to appoint a director to the board of any subsidiary company.
Taken specifically ?
Taken specifically.

It seems to me the explanation given by the Solicitor General in regard to the stocks of the subsidiary companies would be correct if there had been an amalgamation of those companies with the Canadian Northern; but, inasmuch as there is no amalgamation, as the companies are still separate entities, I certainly cannot appreciate his argument that the right to participate in dividends on the stock is in any way militated against by the fact that the Canadian Northern owns it. It makes no difference whether the Canadian Northern or I own the stock. Each company has a separate entity and has so many shares out, and is entitled to earn dividends on those shares. Who is to say that it is not so entitled ? The fact that those shares are owned by the Canadian Northern and that the Canadian Northern is under a cer-
[Jir. Meighen.]
tain agreement with this Government has no more to do with the case than if I owned the shares. I repeat, my hon. friend's argument would be sound if those companies were merged in the Canadian Northern, but' my hon. friend has, by these resolutions, carefully provided that the subsidiary companies shall not be merged with the Canadian Northern but that they shall retain their separate entities in every particular. Therefore, I maintain that their shares still will have a perfect right to earn dividends.

My view is exactly the opposite. I maintain that if there had been an amalgamation my explanation would be utterly false. The stocks would then be wiped out entirely. There has not been an amalgamation, but in so far as capitalization is concerned, as a power to call for dividends, exactly the same results have been achieved. My hon. friend says that the Canadian Northern Ontario may come and say: We want dividends on this $10,000,000. How can the Canadian Northern Ontario come? The only people that can come are the owners of the stock. Who are the owners of the stock? The Canadian Northern Railway Company. The Canadian Northern Railway Company come and say: We want dividends. Very well, we answer the Canadian Northern Railway Company:	You
exchanged your stock for Canadian Northern Ontario stock and paid for it by giving this stock; you gave $23,000,000 of stock for this $68,000,000 in the other company and there is only $100,000,000 of stock that has now the right to call for dividends. If they say: We want dividends on this stock as well, the answer is immediate:	You are
asking for dividends on the $68,000,000 and on the $23,000,000 as well that you gave for it. The $100,000,000 is all that can call for dividends because the $100,000,000 is the total capitalization of the company.

The argument of my hon. friend does not show that he has much faith in the success of the enterprise because he always argues as if the enterprise were to be a failure and that the company would not be able to discharge its liabilities out of the funds at its disposal. The argument of the hon. gentleman against my proposition is certainly that the words which are used in this clause are quite sufficient to protect the public against the demands of the stockholders. He said- and it is a part of the argument itself-

that the company cannot selil the stock of the subsidiary companies because nobody would buy it; it would go into the treasury of the company not only for the $45,000,000 of a mortgage that we are creating but for the $331,000,000 of liabilities already existing. Very true, but suppose the enterprise is profitable, that the Canadian Northern railway discharge not only the mortgage we 'axe taking now of $45,000,000 but discharge the previous mortgage of $312,000,000, what is to prevent them from selling that stock? What have you to say against it? The Government may say that because the Government are interested they have it in their power to prevent it but suppose the securities have been discharged what would be the situation? Then the company have it in their power to sell that stock and put it as a charge against the road. Who is going to prevent it suppose the enterprise proves profitable? My hon. friend ought to look into that matter and see that it is made clear that the company cannot dispose of that stock in any way whatever. My hon. friend said that the stock would be wiped away. That was the interpretation he gave to it because if he did not pretend that the stock would be wiped away certainly he conveyed the impression that the stock would be concentrated in the hands of the owners and would remain there for no purpose whatever either good or bad. If that stock remains there and if the entorprse ie successful what is there to prevent the road from being charged with the $81,000,000 that this stock represents?

The point of my right hon. friend is that in the event of the paying off of the liabilities the sale of the stock would be a business possibility And there is nothing to prevent it. There is no way in tire world of paying tbA=e liabilities except by refunding of mortgages. Railway liabilities do not diminish as a rule with an increase of business, even with successful railways. The road may be a success and yet its indebtedness may increase. A refunding mortgagee would undoubtedly call for all these securities and for .all these stocks of this and the other roads. He would not likely advance enough to pay off the total indebtedness and leave some of the securities out. But in the next place even if he did, we have an interest in this transaction because we are becoming stockholders to the extent of two-fifths of the enterprise and 269*
we will have an interest in any refunding operations and the paying off of old debts. We will be in a position to call upon the courts to enforce that clause and that clause says what the Canadian Northern shall have in its treasury. If those stocks remain there they do not pass out of the treasury. I see no practical likelihood of danger arising in this connection and it would appear that the words are sufficient.

Jt seems to me that the hon. Solicitor General is not looking ahead sufficiently with a view to protecting the public interest. We know very well that circumstances change rapidly in a new and growing country like Canada and the time may come when the Canadian Northern railway would wish to have a refunding or consolidation of their securities. They might be able to wipe off the existing securities by issuing new ones. We know that the rate of interest changes. It was only a few years ago the Government of New Brunswick made an issue of bonds bearing only three per cent interest and received 96 net for them. To-day the Canadian Government, with all its resources, is unable to sell its four per cent debentures at more than par. In a few year's money may be more plentiful and it may be desirable to refund these securities at a lower rate. The time may come when it would be to the advantage of the Canadian Northern Railway Company to dispose of the stock of the subsidiary and constituent companies which they are to hold in the treasury amounting to $681,000,000. The resolution ought to be amended so as to provide for all time that the stocks should remain in the treasury of the Canadian Northern Railway Company, that they should not be disposed of and that neither in respect to the tolls which they can take out of the people nor for any other purpose should they have a value except as is represented by the issued stock of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. It would be very easy to frame an amendment that would cover that and the public would know that the total capitalization of the Canadian Northern, including the capitalization of the constituent companies, will not exceed the capitalization of the Canadian Northern as it may be fixed by Parliament. But the Solicitor General says that If application should be made to the Board of Railway Commissioners and if they should be asked to consider the stock of the subsidiary companies, the Board of Railway Commissioners would say:	You

cannot do that because the stock of the Canadian Northern was issued in consideration of the stock of these constituent companies. There is the difficulty. It was not. Last year $7,000,000 of stock was issued and paid up, the Minister of Finance says, and that was issued in consideration of the payment to the company of a bonus of $15,000,000 or $16,000,000. Therefore, the company might very well say to the Board of Railway Commissioners, that $7,000,000 belongs to the Government and the Government might very well s"ay it too because consideration. was given for it. As to the increase now that is proposed of the sum of $23,000,000, and indeed of the sum of $43,000,000; because $25,000,000 of stock is being provided for in order to take the place of the controvertible income debentures,- the company would say: There is a perfect consideration because that was the arrangement we made with the Government when they guaranteed our bonds under which arrangement Mackenzie, Mann and Company were to have $60,000,000 and the Government were to have $40,000,000.
They may say that was issued for a different consideration altogether from these stocks of the constituent companies. If these stocks are to become the property of the Canadian Northern Railway Company, surely the Canadian Northern can dispose of. their own property, as the board of directors may deem desirable. They could encumber it; they could encumber the equity of redemption in it; they could give a second mortgage on it next year, the same as they are giving a second, third and fourth mortgage now upon many of the assets of the Canadian Northern. There is nothing in the question of a second, third or fourth mortgage that would prevent Mackenzie and Mann from getting money in the money markets of the world. The very fact that this stock, amounting to $81,000,000, was encumbered by a mortgage of $45,000,000, would not prevent Mackenzie, Mann and Company from going to the money markets of the world and floating a second mortgage. Supposing this mortgage is wiped out and another mortgage placed on the assets of the company which would not cover the stock of the constituent companies, what would prevent the Canadian Northern from disposing of this $81,000,000 worth of stock? The important point to the people of this country is that the total capitalized stock that is to be considered at any time should not exceed the capitalization of the Canadian North-
QMr. Pugsley.]
ern railway. If my hon. friend the Solicitor General and the Government really believe that this should be so, why not amend section 3 by adding at the end of paragraph b the following words:
It shall not be lawful for the Canadian Northern to transfer the equity of redemption in said shares of stock or any of them during the pendency of said mortgage, nor at any time thereafter, to transfer the said shares of stock or any of them. All such shares of stock, as well as the physical property of said companies shall be deemed to be represented by the issued capital stock of the Canadian Northern, and the said shares shall not at any time or for any purpose be deemed to have a value apart from or beyond their value as represented by and included in the issued capital stock of the Canadian Northern.
If my hon. friend will amend the section in that way, he 'will avoid all possible question. I am greatly impressed ,by what my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition has said. It is open to that construction; and there is a very great danger in the future that, in justifying the charging of high tolls the company may be able to say to the Railway Commissioners: You have to take the capitalization of all these constituent companies, a matter of $81,000,000, and the capitalization of the Canadian Northern, representing $100,000,000 more. That makes a total capitalization of $181,000,000, upon which it may well be argued that the Canadian Northern will be entitled to earn dividends, and so justify higher tolls upon the road. I would think, if the Government is sincere, as I believe they are-I have no reason to question their sincerity-they will consent to make it so clear that the man who runs may read, and that there will be no opportunity for lawyers to argue about it. I will send the amendment to my right hon. friend if he is disposed to consider it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I must say that the result which my hon. friend desires to provide by the amendment he proposes is already achieved by the language of the section, as follows:
Such shares to become and to remain the property of the Canadian Northern.

As Mackenzie, Mann
and Company's property is going into the Canadian Northern, is not that as 'between Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, and the Canadian Northern? Between the two, it is to he the property and to remain the property of the Canadian Northern.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I really cannot see it just in that way. The words ' to remain ' must

have a certain office. The office they fulfil, as I understand it, is exactly that described by the Solicitor General. I think that the language is quite sufficient as it is. If my hon. friend will allow this clause to pass, I will undertake to come back to it at any time, and in the meantime I will consider his amendment. .

Will the Solicitor General explain why the item of $2,940,000 of stock held by Mackenzie, Mann and Company and associates in the Duluth, Winnipeg and Pacific Railway Company, as set forth on page 34 of the blue-book, is not included in this schedule? All the rest of the stock set forth on this page of the blue-book is included in the schedule.

The reason is this. This is a road in the United States, and it is in the interest of the Canadian Northern to control it. Mackenzie, Mann and Company have been at very considerable expense to purchase this stock, and at present money is owed by them to acquire the stock. If we take it, we shall have to discharge that indebtedness, and we did not feel that a sufficient object was to be served as would warrant so great an outlay at the present time.
Then why did you take $3,060,000 of the stock?
That is the controlling interest.

I am not able to follow my hon. friend. He says that he takes the controlling interest, but he does not take the whole of it for fear that we may be called upon to pay the 9 p.m. liabilities. If my hon. friend's reasoning is good, we are going far enough to compel the Government to assume the liabilities, and yet we leave practically one-half of the assets in the hands of Mackenzie, Mann and Company.

My hon. friend has
misunderstood me. This road is a feeder for the Canadian Northern, and it is in the interest of the Canadian Northern to control the road. Consequently we acquire a controlling interest in it, which is represented by the $3,060,000, or about 51 per cent. The other stock has since been purchased by Mackenzie, Mann and Company with their own resources; and as I understand it, the money is owing, the stock being pledged as security for it, and we, of course, would have to pay that amount to get the rest of that stock. We did not feel
that a sufficient object was to be served to warrant the cash outlay at the present time. We have control without it.

Does my hon. friend
mean to say that, while Mackenzie, Mann and Company ostensibly have ownership of $2,940,000 worth of stock, yet they owe the money for it and somebody else has a lien upon the stock? It does not say so here. If it did, it would be some little-evidence that Mackenzie, Mann and Company were giving something to the Government of Canada in the way of security. The mere fact that they may happen to owe some money on it does not seem to be any reason why the people of Canada have not the assets, whatever they may be.

We could not get the stock as security until we discharged the liability. It will be discharged when Mackenzie and Mann pay for it. We did not feel that a sufficient object would be served in getting the minority stock to warrant the cash outlay, because we have the control of the road without it. We felt that, especially as the road was in the United States.
The blue-book says that this road is held by Mackenzie, Mann and associates.
They are the beneficial owners.

My hon. friend says
that that is not true; that they have only some sort of a right in it, and that the stock is subject to a lien to somebody else. Does the Solicitor General say that Mackenzie, Mann and Company now own it; or do they hold it subject to a lien, and have we to pay the lien to get it?

I know they are the
beneficial owners-; and I can assure my hon. friend, with practically no reservation, that they do owe a large amount against it, if not the purchase price. Aside from that, whether they owed it or not, we would have to pay what they paid for it. The Canadian Northern railway could not ask for it otherwise than to pay what they had paid to secure the debt. We did not feel the cash value was warranted inasmuch as we have control of the road and fifty-one per cent without it.
What about the question of rates? Would not the minority of the stockholders have something to say about the rates we must charge?
That is in the United States.
Not the whole of it.

Yes. It runs to Fort Francis. I have not been there except going through on the train, but I think the American border comes right to the river at Fort Francis, and this road runs from Duluth to Virginia in Minnesota and from Virginia to Fort Francis.
Subsection b agreed to.
On section 3, subsection c:
(c)	There shall be conveyed to the trustees as part of the specifically first mortgaged premises, by the purchaser at court sale thereof, the railway and undertaking mentioned in the third part of the second schedule hereto, the said railway and undertaking to be free from all bonds or other indebtedness thereon, the same to become the property of the Canadian Northern subject to the mortgage or charge created by the new trust deed, and to be operated by the Canadian Northern as part of its system.
That is the transfer absolutely of the railway?

That is the Brockville and Westport.
Subsection c agreed to.
On section 3, subsection d:
(d)	There shall be transferred to the Minister of Finance and Receiver General of Canada in trust for the Government of Canada, three hundred and thirty thousand fully paid shares of the par value of $100 each of the capital stock of the Canadian Northern and such shares shall be the absolute property of His Majesty in right of the Dominion of Canada. The said shares or any part thereof may be disposed of under the authority of Parliament upon such terms and conditions as it may determine, and the proceeds of the sale thereof paid into the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada. Pending the disposal of the said shares and of the shares issued to the Minister of Finance and Receiver General of Canada, pursuant to section 8 of chapter 10 of the statutes of 1913, all voting and other rights under the said shares shall be exercisable by the minister or by whomsoever he may from time to time appoint.

This clause raises the question of partnership. The Minister of Finance' objects to the assertion that a partnership is involved. At the same time he claims a great deal of credit for the Government for making an arrangement by which the country will have a forty per cent	interest	in
the profits of this enterprise. Now, I am not concerned whether it is called a partnership or shareholding, but what concerns me is how far the holding of this forty per

cent supposedly of the shares of this company will carry the Government in responsibility for the enterprise. Are they going to take this position-that having only a minority of the shares they have no responsibility for the conduct of the enterprise -or are they going to assume the position that having forty per cent of the shares and the dominant right in the enterprise as the principal creditor they will assume the general responsibility for its conduct and result?
I can only say, we are not going to assume general responsibility for its conduct and result. We are simply shareholders to t'he extent of forty per cent of its stock.

The Government, then, is assuming the position of silent partner, and paying partner in this company and disclaims any responsibility for the conduct of the enterprise but only the right of putting up the money.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Of course the Government is not assuming the management of the road. If we assumed that we should have to go into the question of government operation. The arrangement which we have made is based, in the first place, upon the view expressed by many hon. gentlemen on the other side that we could not allow this railway, a railway to which so much support has been given not only by the federal Parliament but by the provincial parliaments, to collapse and remain uncompleted. I need not discuss that now for it has been discussed at length already. That being the case, it was necessary to consider on what basis the assistance should be given. We thought the various roads of the system should be amalgamated as far as was possible iin view of their varied financial arrangements. That has been accomplished so far as we thought it possible to accomplish it by the transfer of the stock to which I have alluded. In the next place we thought the capitalization of the road should be reduced to a sum not exceeding $100,000,000. That also has been accomplished in the way I pointed out. We thought that if the country came to the assistance of the road at this time to secure its completion, it was proper that the country should participate in a reasonable way in the advantages of the enterprise, should it in the end prove successful, as we all hope, and most of us believe. Therefore, we insisted on the transfer of

$33,000,000 of stock to the Government, in order that the country may obtain that advantage. Had we acquired the majority of the stock we should have had to assume the management of the enterprise. It did not seem desirable to do that.
iMr. OLIVER: The essential point is, aside from the little transaction of last year, it changes the position from that of debtor and creditor to that of partner and creditor. That is a very radical change in status-and there is no doubt about it, because it has been reiterated by members on the other slide from the Finance Minister and the Prime Minister himself down-that the Government is henceforward to have an interest in the success of the enterprise altogether aside from the ordinary interest of a government representing the whole people. I am merely asking what effect the change has in the relative position of the Government and the company as changing the relation from that of debtor and creditor to that olf junior partner and creditor. And what effect will that change have upon the general relationship of the Government to the enterprise?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not know that it
will mean any particular change in the relationship. The country through the Government had a very pronounced interest in the enterprise; if the undertaking were successful, the Government, having expended certain moneys by way of subsidies in the construction of the road and having also guaranteed bonds for a considerable amount, naturally would have a marked financial interest in the success of the road, apart altogether from the advantage which must accrue to the country if the road be carried on successfully as a transcontinental railway. The only difference now resulting is this: that apart from the financial aspect to which I have just alluded, the people will have a certain share in the success of the road, if it proves successful, by reason of their interest in the stock issue.

Do I understand my right hon. friend to say that by getting two-flfths of the stock of this enterprise the Government do not impose upon themselves as the trustees of the people of Canada the duty of looking after this company, of being represented at its meetings and of voting in the selection of directors? Does he say that the trustees of the people may
abstain from any part in the direction of the affairs of the company?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I say that the Government are not undertaking the management of the road. The road is left under the management of the Canadian Northern Railway Company, as before.

If anything in these
resolutions is objectionable-and a good many things are-this provision is the most objectionable of all.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Which one?

The provision that the Government shall become the owner of two-fifths of the stock of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. Call it what you like, the effect is that the Government enters into partnership with Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, in this enterprise; Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, are to own three-fifths of the stock and the Government are to own two-fifths. If two people join together in promoting an undertaking of this kind, one man taking three-fifths of the stock and the other man taking two-fifths, they became partners in the undertaking; the fact that it is a joint stock company does not alter the position at all. If this legislation passes, the Government of Canada commit the people of this country to a voic^ in the management of the affairs of this company; they impose upon themselves as trustees of the people the duty of being represented at the meetings, the duty of voting for the choice of directors, the duty of taking a part in the management of the company. If anything goes wrong, the Government cannot say that they were in the minority and that they therefore abstained from taking any part in the management of the company. It is their duty, just as it would be the duty of any trustee holding two-fifths of the capital stock of a company, to take a part in the management in order to see that the interests of those, for whom they are acting are properly safeguarded.

May I ask the hon. gentleman if he will cite some work on partnership in jwhiioh at is stated that if the senior or majority partner does not make the thing pay, he has to collapse in favour of the junior partner?

The question which my hon. friend puts is marked by the wisdom which is usually displayed in every

question he puts to the House or to the committee, but it does not seem to be apropos of the point which I wish to make; therefore my hon. friend will pardon me if I do not take the time to answer him.
What a farce it was last year that the Government, when they gave the bonus to the Canadian Northern Railway Company took $7,000,000 of the company's capital stock and made the people of Canada the owners of stock to that extent. Last year the Minister of Finance took a great deal of credit to himself for taking that stock, the cost of which was simply the cost of the paper and the time of the printer in striking off stock certificates representing that amount. It was argued from this side of the House, that that was a worthless security and what has taken place during this session shows how absolutely worthless was the stock which the Minister of Finance took at that time. At the present time, with the $7,000,000 taken last year, the capital stock of the company is $77,000,000. Out of that amount there are to be reserved $25,000,000 which the holders of convertible income debenture stock may exchange for their stock. That would leave the difference between $25,000,000 and $77,000,000 as the actually issued capital stock to-day, some $52,000,000. It is now proposed to increase the capital stock to $100,000,000; to make an increase of $48,000,000 of watered stock in this company, and it is proposed to give the Government of Canada $33,000,000 of this watered stock and to make their holdings $40,000,000 in all. I submit that if it is in the interests of the1 sections of the country through which this1 system passes and in the interests of Canada as a whole that the Candian Northern Railway Company should be aided a,t the present time, let the application stand upon its own merits; let aid be given in the interests of the country, but do not let the Government go into the speculation of taking this common stock. The country does not want it. If the country wants to aid this enterprise, it will do it because it is desirable to secure competition; because it is desirable to have this transcontinental! railway completed. But the gentlemen upon the other side are really putting forward the contention that they axe doing this because for one reason they are getting $33,000,000 of stock which they are going to lay away in the treasury in the hope that in 25 or perhaps 50 years the stock may be of some 
value. I say that the action of the Government should be influenced by one consideration only, and that is the desirability of completing this transcontinental system in the interests of the various communities to be served and in the interests of the whole of the people of Canada. Yet, as a consideration for doing this, the Government is to take $33,000,000 of additional stock which is to be laid away, as I have said, in the hope that the people will ultimately get some consideration for having aided this railway company. I submit that that is an entirely erroneous principle. This Government is going into partnership with Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, and they cannot escape responsibility for the management of this company's affairs. When Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, hereafter go into the markets of the world to finance further this enterprise they will be able to say with the utmost truth to financial men, when they are asked who owns the Canadian Northern railway: His Majesty the King and we own it; we own three-fifths of it; His Majesty the King, as represented by the Government of Canada, owns two-fifths of it. On behalf of His Majesty and on behalf of themselves they will ask the financiers of the world to deal with them in respect of this enterprise. The very moment the Government of Canada become interested as holders of the common stock of this company, that moment they engage as partners in this enterprise, that moment they pledge themselves to the people of Canada and the financial people of the world who are interested in [DOT] the railway to do their part in securing an efficient and proper management of this railway; and they, the Government of Canada, will be just as responsible for the proper and efficient management of this road as Mackenzie, Mann and Company will be. The Prime Minister has left it to be understood that we are to have nothing to do with the management because it is to be in the hands of Mackenzie, Mann and Company. But by this very paragraph it is provided that all voting and other rights attaching to the shares shall be exercised by the Minister of Finance and the Receiver General, or by whomsoever he may from time to time appoint. Does that not mean that they will take part, be represented at meetings, that they are to exercise influence on the Board of Directors, and that as shareholders, as trustees for the people of Canada and as having a right to vote for

directors they are to exercise diligence and care and judgment in the management of the affairs of this company? From the moment they become, as trustees for the people of Canada, interested to the extent of two-fifths of the capital stock, I say they cannot escape the duty of taking part in its management and cannot escape responsibility to the financial world or to the people of Canada for the way in which that railroad is managed. I desire to give notice that after this resolution leaves the committee and when it comes up on concurrence, I shall move that instead of taking this stock, the capital stock shall be reduced and not increased by watered stock to the extent of forty odd million dollars; that it shall be reduced to what anybody would say is a fair value of the equity of redemption in this property. When I spoke the other day I said from $5,000,000 to $10,000,000 would be ample; but by reason of the fact that there is a call for $25,000,000, and it is necessary that the stock should be more than that, I am willing to make it $30,000,000. But that will reduce it bv $70,000,000. That will wipe out, if my views be acceded to, $70,000,000 of this common stock upon which the people of the country who are to send their traffic over this railway, may have to pay the interest in the way of increased tolls. I reduce it down to $30,000,000, at the same time leaving provision for the exchange of the income debenture stock to the extent of the $25 000 000 which is referred to in the resolution.' I would provide that that $30,000,000 of stock as so reduced should be placed in the hands of the Receiver General and held by him for the period of five years. That will give, ample time to test whether or not this enterprise can be successfully carried through. I would leave in the hands of the nominee of Mackenzie, Mann and Company sufficient stock to qualify the directors that may be chosen. I would provide that, in case no default is made by the company m the payment of interest, and in ease the conditions of the resolution and agreement shall be carried out for the period of five years, and in case His Majesty shall not exercise the option which my amendment provides for, the stock shall be handed back to Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, or their nominees. Then I would provide that at any time within the period of five years the Governor in Council would have the right to acquire the absolute ownership of- the stock of the Canadian Northern and of all the constituent and subsidiary companies, thus vesting the entire ownership in His Majesty, subject to existing encumbrances and the right of the holders of debenture stock to receive their $25,000,000. I would allow in the meantime the control to be in Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited. If that were done it would simply place the Government in the position in which they ought to be placed, giving them security upon this stock as the holders for five years. If during that time there should be no default, then the stock would be handed1 back unless His Majesty chose to exercise the option of taking the road over. But I think now is the time, when the Canadian Northern, railway is coming to the Government and asking for this enormous .aid-, when they recognize that they cannot get through their financial difficulties unless aid is given, now is the time for the Government to secure an option upon the entire stock of this road. Hon. gentlemen may say that there is no need of making that provision. I say that there is, because the feeling of the people of Canada to-day is, I think, rapidly growing in favour of having a Government-owned railway system extending across this continent. The Government are operating the Intercolonial railway, and, while it is the fashion with many of the people of this -country to disparage the Government operation of that road, I say its operation is very successful indeed. While there is some complaint, yet, upon the whole, the Intercolonial railway is managed in such a w.ay as to give general satisfaction to the people. I shall not speak of the exceptional circumstances which have occurred recently under the administration of affairs by the present Minister of Railways and the present manager of the Intercolonial railway; but, speaking generally as to all the years since the Intercolonial railway was constructed, its operation has been very beneficial to the people of the country and 'such as to give general satisfaction. The Government own that system, extending from the eastern part of Nova Scotia -and from the southern part of New Brunswick through to the city of Montreal, and also extending over a large portion of Prince Edward Island. It is a system of about 1,800 miles in length. In the West the Government is carrying out the policy of the late Administration in constructing the Hudson Bay railway. Why might it not be that the people would approve of making an extension of this system so as

to take in the Canadian Northern railway? I would not bind the 'Government to do it to-day, but I would give to the Government the option of doing it if the people of the country, at any time within five years, should declare it to be their judgment that the road should be taken over. As to whether that would be just to Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, or not, I submit it would be. If the Government should exercise its option and take the road ovct at any time before the end of five years at a price to be fixed by arbitration but not exceeding $30,000,000, I think that would be treating them as fairly and with as great a degree of justice as they could reasonably ask for. If the Government should decide not to take it over, the stock would be handed back to Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, or their nominees. The proposition which I make is, of course, entirely different from the proposal which the Government are putting forward. The Government are becoming a junior partner in this undertaking, they are becoming the absolute owners of two-fifths of the common stock, leaving outstanding $50,000,000 -of stock, three-fifths in the hands of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited. If the enterprise is successful by reason of the aid which the Government are now giving, that stock before five years have rolled away may have a very considerable value. It may or it may not, but at all events it may get into the hands of third parties. The stock may be so widely scattered that it will be impossible to secure it except by expropriation and it might be exceedingly difficult for the Government to acquire ownership of the system. Under the plan which I suggest, the Government could take an option upon this stock and hold it for five years. If Mackenzie, Mann and Company, pull the enterprise through, the stock is handed back to them unless the Government choose to take over the road under the provisions of the option for which this amendment would provide.
I have listened to all that has been said with regard to the present proposition, and the more I think of it the more objectionable it seems. I have heard' from business men in different parts of Canada and I do not believe you will find a business or railway man in the country, outside of those who are specially interested in the Canadian Northern, who approves of the proposition of this Country becoming a partner with Mackenzie and Mann in this enterprise and taking over its stock. On the other hand, there is a general disposition

that the enterprise, although it ought to be aided and not allowed to go down, should be aided in the way of guaranteeing the securities and in the way of .having the stock held as security until the enterprise has been made a success.

We are always glad to have any suggestions from the hon. member for St. John and particularly glad to have a new railway policy enunciated by him on behalf, I presume, of the Liberal party in the House of Commons. I presume this is in succession to and in substitution of the policy of the leader of the Opposition.
At the present time I am speaking for myself.

And it is supposed, I presume, to be an improvement on the policy of the hon. member for South Renfrew, the ex-Minister of Railways. However suggestions were asked for when the resolution to go into committee was moved, and are thankfully received, and if there is any new policy from the Opposition the sooner it comes forward the better. In relation to what my hon. friend suggests that this proposal should embody the stipulation that the stocks shall be put in the hands of the Receiver General, in trust, so that in the event of success Canada will be able to exercise the option of purchase, the hon. member is sufficient a lawyer to know that we have no such power in this House except by the consent of the parties interested, because we have no control of civil rights. We could make it a condition of aid, but the hon. gentleman has also business judgment enough to know that to suggest it to the parties interested would be simply received as a joke. The policy of my hon. friend means nothing more than allowing this system to go into the hands of a receiver just as rapidly as it will, and the Dominion of Canada and the provinces being called on to make good their guarantees after the road is in the hands of a receiver. This policy is the direct opposite of the policy of the leader of the Opposition, who says that we must not allow this road to go into the hands of a receiver, and directly the opposite of the policy of the hon. member for South Renfrew, who agrees with the leader of the Opposition that we must not allow the road to go into the hands of a receiver. Let me repeat that such a proposal to the owners of the stock of the Canadian Northern and of the subsidiary companies would appeal to them as it

would appeal to anybody else, as being perfectly absurd.
Why?

For such a multitude of reasons that the night is too short to enumerate them. As if Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann would undertake the responsibility of taking hold of the Canadian Northern and financing it to success, and give to the people of Canada the option of taking the road over if it is a success and reducing their stock to about one-fifth of what has been declared to be fully paid up by a Parliament of this country! Parliament comes along year by year, and by its steps declares that certain stock of this company is paid up, and rightly paid up, or Parliament would not so declare it; and Parliament by its statutes vests that stock in a certain place. Now the hon. gentleman asks us to propose to these men, who have acquired this stock under the sanction of Parliament, that it should be reduced to one-fifth, and that if they make the road pay at all Canada shall have the option of taking the stock from them, and that in the meantime they shall incur the risks of operating the road. I do not know what all the effects of that policy are, but I understand enough of it to know that it means the steady march of this system to a receivership and all the consequences that follow.

I think this is a very remarkable statement.	\Y e have been
able to get mord'information from my hon. friend in the last five minutes than in the last five days, although he was not able to give my hon. friend from St. John a plain answer to a plain question.
Which policy of all the four that have been advanced does my hon. friend from Edmonton support?

I am supporting a policy whereby Mackenzie, Mann and the Government shall maintain their relationship of debtor and creditor; whereby the Government of Canada shall not make itself responsible for the management of the Canadian Northern enterprise unless and until it takes over the ownership of the eji-terprise. Why should it be said that the acceptance by the House of the suggestion of my hon. friend from St. John would mean a receivership for the Canadian Northern? Is it because Mackenzie and Mann would refuse the offer couched in
the terms that have been placed before the House? If that is the reason, we shall have to adjust out point of view all along the line. If they would consider it as a joke, then I think we had better reconsider the proposal that the Government have placed before the House. For my part, I do not consider it a joke at all. If this country is going to stand behind Mackenzie and Mann to the extent of $45,000,000, this country is entitled to have some say as to the terms under which Mackenzie and Mann shall receive that aid-terms that shall hot be dictated by Z. A. Lash nor by Mackenzie and Mann themselves, but by the people of this Dominion.

Who said there was
any dictation? All I said was that we could not compel such an arrangement inasmuch as we have no control over civil rights. If Mackenzie and Mann prefer the other course thejy have the right to so elect, and in my humble judgment they would so elect.
They would have a perfect right to so elect.
That is not dictation.

They would have the perfect right to treat this proposition as a joke. I think that is what my hon. friend suggested they would do. If that is their attitude, if they think this country has nothing else to do with $45,000,000 than to hand it over to them on their terms, I think the joke is on the Government.
I did not say that at all.

What is there wrong in making terms with Mackenzie and Mann? If we are to supply the money why should we not dictate the terms. This Government is going into partnership with Mackenzie and Mann and while we take two-fifths they get three-fifths; we are allowing them the earning rights on $60,000,000 of common stock while we take the earning rights on $40,000,000. What is there so jocular about saying to Mackenzie and Mann: You can take the whole earning rights on $30,000,000 of common stock, and you are doing well if you get that out of this enterprise, because all the evidence that has been put betfore the House during this discussion goes to 6how that Mackenzie and

Mann, up to date, have not put one solitaxy red cent into the enterprise. I think $30,000,000 would be a very ample reward to these gentlemen, giving them credit for all the enterprise and all the ability that our friends on the other side have asserted them to have.
The hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) does not say that. He '(distinctly repudiated the suggestion that they had put no money into it.

We have had this discussion going on for several days and there has been no evidence offered to this House that Mackenzie, Mann and Company ever put a cent into it, and not only that, but when the suggestion has been made that they should put money into it, the Government has been careful to protect them from that suggestion. I do not think, giving these gentlemen credit for all the ability they have shown, that they are entitled to everything. The country is entitled to something for this money and particularly this Parliament is here to make such terms with Mackenzie and Mann, or anybody else who has to deal with it, as shall be in the public interest; and it is not in the public interest that, in' the case of an enterprise such as this which has been constructed by the contributions and the credit, in a large majority, of the people of Canada, there should be $100,000,000 of common stock outstanding upon which dividends should be>
earned.
I was .anxious, before my hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley) gave notice of his resolution, to get from the Government a statement of their policy having regard to the interest which they propose to take in the enterprise. I want to ask them now, in the matter of the regulation of railway rates: Are they going to treat that question as having a financial interest in the maintenance of high rates on the system, or are they going to, as a matter of policy, ignore the interest that as partners in the enterprise they would have and treat the question outside of that altogether? This is a matter of fundamental importance to the people of the country. The papers of Canada are full of the assertion that, now that the Government are going into partnership with this great railway system, the railway companies are thereby protected from the reduction of their rates because it will be the interest of the Government to keep up the rates in oeder to kep up the irevenue.

Again, I am anxious to know what the Government's policy is in regard to the ex-' tension of branch lines in the prairie provinces. For two years construction on these branch lines has been practically at a standstill. The provincial governments have undertaken immense responsibilities. The Alberta Government has given a guarantee, I believe, to the amount of about $20,000,000 to this company for the construction of branch lines in connection with its system. These lines are not constructed. Hundreds of miles which have been guaranteed are untouched to-day. The outstanding guarantees are not sufficient, I am credibly informed, to complete these lines. I want to know if the Government, as partners with Mackenzie, Mann and Company, are going to see that these lines are completed. Are they going to see to the further extension of these lines which is absolutely called for? At the present time Mackenzie and Mann, enterprising railroaders though they are, have started a number of railway lines all radiating from Edmonton. They have occupied the territory near Edmonton but it is the country farther beyond that needs and demands accommodation. Are these enterprises to be allowed to remain where they are, practically holding up the development of the country farther on, or are the Government, as partners in this enterprise, going to take the responsibility of pushing these branches out to the people who need railway communication so much? In reference to the matters of railway rates and railway extension wd want to know what the policy of the Government is going to be as partners in this enterprise? What interest are they going to take in these two important matters? It is necessary that we .should know what their policy is going to be. My view is that the Government should not be partners in the enterprise, that they should occupy the position of creditor as against the company's position of debtor so long as there is a reasonable probability of the debtor being able to carry this enterprise through and then, if he fails in carrying this enterprise through, having been given the assistance that might reasonably be given, this Government must assume the responsibility for the enterprise altogether and take it up as a Government project. It should either belong to the company or it should belong to the Government; there should be no partnership as between the company and the Government.

On section 4:
That covenants or undertakings to the satisfaction of the Governor in Council shall be given that all outstanding temporary loans to the Canadian Northern or any of its constituent or subsidiary companies secured by the deposit or pledge of securities, will be paid out of the proceeds of such deposited or pledged securities when the same shall be sold or disposed of, and that no proceedings against the Canadian Northern or any of said other companies will meanwhile be taken for the collection of such temporary loans.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The Bill is going to make that a condition precedent. It does not stand that way in the resolution. Therefore, I would move to amend the clause by striking out the word ' four ' and substituting the letter ' e.'
Has the Solicitor General anything to say upon this?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The purport of it is merely to make these covenants a condition precedent to the guarantee.

This and the other section have been discussed in anticipation. By the two clauses the contractors undertake to give the Government a satisfactory covenant that their creditors, whether they be the banks or other companies, shall not press them for payment and that they will reduce their indebtedness to what is admitted to be the current amount of liability between railway company and railway company. In the next place, they undertake to obtain from the contractors a covenant that the banks will be satisfied to wait, if they have to wait, for a certain period of time. At the present time the banks are secured by pledges in their hands amounting to $24,000,000 covering a liability of $21,000,000. Any covenant that these parties give must satisfy the Government but it may not satisfy the banks. If, however, they can satisfy the banks what reason have they to come to the Government?
At the present time the ibanks -are well secured with the guarantees which they have in hand; but as I understand it, the securities will not be and cannot be liquidated at present, perhaps on account of the condition of the m-arket, and they would therefore, have to stand over. In that case, what covenant can Mackenzie and Mann give to the Government which will satisfy the Government if they cannot satisfy the banks?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: They can give security in many different forms. They can give us the security of a bank, of a guarantee company, or of a bond.
Exactly. They can give all that to the bank. If they can satisfy the bank, certainly they can satisfy the Government; but if they cannot satisfy the bank, how are they to satisfy the Government?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am not sure that the bank is not satisfied at the present time.
If it is, there is no reason for Mackenzie and Mann to come here.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am not sure of that.
There are certain securities, and there is a certain indebtedness. The securities may meet that indebtedness or they may not meet it. What we desire to guard against is that there shall be no embarrassment to the company; that there shall be no action against the company in respect of any of these loans; that they shall be taken care of, and that we shall be satisfied that they shall be taken care of.

I understand all that. Of course, if the bank is satisfied, there will be no action. If the bank is not paid, but is given satisfactory security, there will be no action. In other words, if the bank is satisfied, nothing will be done; but the puzzle to me is what covenant Mackenzie and Mann can give to the Government which will satisfy the Government, if they cannot satisfy the bank. In reply to this I have not received any answer.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Suppose they come to us with the guarantee of a company worth $100,000,000 as security that there should be no proceedings upon that -debt, and that it -should he paid out of these s-e-curities or paid otherwise; should we not accept that security, satisfied that the guarantor was perfectly good for it?

If they went to the bank with a security of $100,000,000, the bank would say:	All right. There
would be no trouble at all.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If they came to us, we would also say: All right.

Why is it that my hon. friend frames the phraseology of sec-tiojn 4 with regard to covenants or undertakings differently from the phraseology of

section 5, where he specially provides that the contractor shall be one of the guarantors? Under section 4 the thing is made general without any reference to the contractors. For the proper understanding of the value of this section and of the position of the securities, I think the Solicitor General, w'ho has intimated to the House that he has in his brief a statement as to when these loans from the bank fall due, should give us that statement now. The items are not so very numerous.
I can give it.
In the meantime, in regard to the other point, is there any reason why the contractors are excluded from section 4 and included in section 5?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If they would give to us satisfactory security under section 4, it would not make any great difference whether they were liable or not. It is necessary that Mackenzie and Mann, Limited, acting as the construction department of the Canadian Northern railway, should have a certain line of credit. My hon. friend will appreciate1 that. It would not be in the interest of completing the enterprise that their credit should be unduly hampered.

Will my right hon.
friend tell me why Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann are called the contractors in the agreement, and yet are not called the contractors in the resolution? According to the agreement the parties of the fourth part are Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald D. Mann, thereinafter called the contractors.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: They were added in the agreement, as has already been explained, for the reason that we thought it desirable in the agreement that we should have their individual and personal release of the claims.
That is 10 p.m. the date of the mortgage.

The table does not give the due date. I will get it.
On section 5:
That covenants or undertakings of the contractors and such other covenants or undertakings as may be required by the Governor in Council shall be given that the current indebtedness of the Canadian Northern and of the said constituent and subsidiary companies will within one year from the passing of the Act to be based upon these resolutions be reduced to the normal or usual current amount to be determined by the minister and that meanwhile all such current indebtedness other than such as may be the subject of bona fide dispute, will be either paid or arranged in such a manner that no proceedings for the enforcement of payment thereof will be taken or pressed.
Will this also become part of section 3 ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes, I desire to strike out the number ' 5 ' and substitute ' f.'

The explanation why my right hon. friend gave for excluding the contractors from section 4 does not seem to me altogether sound, because there is no provision for placing the onus on some particular party that the guarantee shall be given. It is true it is made a provision of the agreement. Unless my hon. friend says that, as a matter of drafting, he does not want to repeat the obligation as resting upon the contractors, I can see no reason why he should not include it in this, just as he has done in the other one, because whose duty is it to give the guarantee except the contractors ? Is the Canadian Northern to do it ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think my hon. friend is right, that they must look after it in some way or other. They have preferred it in this form, and I do not see any objection to it, because we can call upon them under section 4, if we desire to do so; but there is some point in the suggestion made on their behalf that, if they are going to provide capital for, what I have called for the purpose of convenience, construction work for the completion of the road, they must have some credit with the bank, and they think this is the better form to adopt.

Apparently these
securities were pledged to the bank by the Canadian Northern railway, and not by Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited. Therefore it would be the duty of the Can-

adian Northern Railway Company to give the guarantees, not Mackenzie and Mann.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes, I think my hon. friend is right as to that.

These liabilities in section 5 are all the liabilities which are to be found on page 43, namely, Canadian Northern Railway Company; Canadian Northern Ontario railway; Canadian Northern Quebec railway; Quebec and Lake St. John railway; Duluth, Winnipeg and Pacific railway; Halifax and Southwestern Railway Company; Central Ontario railway; Bay of Quinte railway; Irondale, Bancroft and Ottawa railway; Brockville, Westport and Northwestern railway.
These are the companies whose floating liabilities are to be reduced to what is understood to be the ordinary liabilities of such companies. What is to be the amount of current liabilities assumed as normal? I understood the Prime Minister spoke of $2,000,000 or 33,000,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My right hon. friend will observe that the normal amount is to be determined by the Minister of Finance. 1 have already said, I think, it has been represented to us by the officials of the department that the normal or usual current liability of a system such as this would be about $3,000,000.
I would like the Solicitor General to give us the information, if he has it, in brief. Otherwise it would be out of place in the record.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Perhaps we might go on to another section, and give it afterwards, if the hon. gentleman has no objection?
On section 6:
That the kind of securities to be guaranteed hereunder, and the forms thereof, and the forms and terms of the new trust deed, and the times and manner of the issue of the guaranteed securities, and the disposition of the moneys to be raised thereon by sale, pledge or otherwise, and the forms and manner of guarantee or guarantees shall be such as the Governor in Council approves, and such terms, provisions and conditions as the Governor in Council may consider expedient or necessary shall he included in the new trust deed.

I draw attention to the words ' disposition of the moneys to be raised thereon.' I think it is in order here for me to ask how far the Canadian Northern Railway branch lines in Alberta and Saskatchewan are to be benefited by this guarantee. I take it that the Government assumes responsibility for ' the disposition of the moneys to be raised thereon.'
If I am wrong in my interpretation, of course I shall be glad to be set right; but I ask whether the Government, under section 6, assumes responsibility for the moneys raised under the guarantee? If that is the case, I am anxious to know to what extent the various branch lines in the two larger prairie provinces are intended to participate in the benefit of this expenditure.

The answer to that
would be very long if I were to give it from my place. But I may say that from the statements of 'requirements to complete* which appear in the documents filed and printed, it is shown that the Canadian Northern Alberta is to receive for the purpose of completion $523,959, the Canadian Northern Western, $310,088, the Canadian Northern railway proper $5,402,712, and the Canadian Northern Saskatchewan $457,847. Then, as to exactly what portions' these moneys are to be applied to, and also as to the division of the moneys between the various elements of railway building,- ballasting, rails, right of way, betterments, etc.-these all appear in the supporting statements which follow and which are on the table but are not printed in the blue-book. These are given in the fullest possible detail especially in relation to the Canadian Northern, in the third supporting statement.

I do not know that any
great amount of detail is necessary in order to bring out what I want to know. If the Solicitor General would look at page 19 of the blue-book he would see that there is a measurably detailed statement of the requirements. In that statement, of course, is included a statement in regard to the Canadian Northern Western railway, which is one of those the hon. gentleman has mentioned. The line from Warden to Bra-zeau calls for $310,088 to complete and $45,000 for betterments. This is apparently the only expenditure to be made upon the Canadian Northern Western lines out of this sum.

Of course that by no
means comprises all the lines of the Canadian Northern Railway system in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba.

I quite understand that. I simply want it understood that on the Canadian Northern Western line in Alberta, it is proposed that there shall be expended out of this $45,000,000 of guarantee a matter of only $355,000. That expenditure is made

on the Warden-Brazeau line of which 157 miles of track have been laid and 17 miles are graded but no track laid. Now, the Canadian Northern Western lines in Alberta under provincial guarantee amount to 663 miles, and the guarantees' amount to $10,722,250. All this means, as I understand it, that so far as the Canadian Northern' Western is concerned with its 663 miles of lines, it gets $355,000 out of this fund and the balance will have to be supplied on the provincial Government's guarantee.
The provincial Government has guaranteed different branches of this system at from $13,000 to $25,000 a mile. A $25,000 a mile guarantee has been absorbed in this Brazeau-Warden line, which has been practically completed. The remainder of the lines are in the $13,000, $15,000 and $20,000 a mile guarantee class. According to the statement I have here, on about 300 miles of the lines of this system nothing has been' clone, although the lines have been guaranteed, and on about 160 miles some grading has been done. As I work the figures out, on the mileage of this system yet to be completed there remains *of the provincial Government's guarantee not yet expended about $14,000 a mile, not sufficient to build the lines. I would like to know if, in the contingency that the proceeds of the provincial Government guarantees upon those lines are not sufficient to complete them, this Government will, out of the moneys raised under this guarantee, take any responsibility with regard to the completion of those lines.
Will the hon. gentleman tell me the mileage of the Canadian Northwestern guaranteed by the province of Alberta?

From Onoway to Pine Pass, 100 males, $20,000 a mile. On that section track has been laid on 32 miles, 46 miles have been partially graded, and on 22 miles nothing has been done. From Oliver station to St. Paul de Metis, 100 miles, $13,000 a mile. From Bruderheim towards Vermilion, 30 miles, $13,000 a mile. From Calgary, northeast, 100 miles, $13,000 a mile; from Camrose to Alsask, 80 miles, $13,000 a mile; from Stratheona, southwesterly, 20 miles, $15,000 a mile, and from Blackfalls to Goose Lake line, 63 miles, the guarantee is $13,000 a mile.
