While it appears from the statement of requirements to com- [DOT] plete that the amount that is to go from the funds available on the issue of these

securities to the Canadian Northwestern railway is limited to some $355,000, still it must be remembered first of all that the expenditure of the money on the other western lines, and on eastern lines as well, is of direct advantage to the very district served by the Canadian Northwestern. It is of the utmost importance to the residents along the Canadian Northwestern line that the road be completed to the Pacific coast and that the benefit of the rails leading west from that district to Vancouver be obtained and be brought to bear upon the residents of that district. The hon. gentleman will admit at once that the benefit goes directly and more largely to the residents of Alberta and Saskatchewan under the expenditure on the main lines of road, but in addition this consideration must be kept in mind: provision is made by these resolutions which will leave a great deal of scope for the extension of the branch lines of the Canadian Northern. By the trust deed of June 30, 1903, it is provided that there may be issued, under the authority of and secured by that trust deed, bonds not exceeding $10,000 a mile for any new line constructed. That $10,000 a mile is subject to $15,000 a mile prior charge, provided the $15,000 is guaranteed by the Dominion or by a province, and to $10,000 a mile if it is not so guaranteed. So that in the case of such lines as are guaranteed by the province of Alberta the Canadian Northern Railway Company may . issue bonds up to a total of $25,000 a mile, provided the guaranteed bonds reach $15,000 and that $25,000 a mile I think the hon. gentleman will admit will take care of construction in Alberta. So that as there is left unimpaired the authority to issue securities ahead of the $45,000,000 security, to that extent reasonable encouragement is given and reasonable means are preserved whereby branch lines may be built and all necessary extensions made from time to time.
The Canadian Northern is allowed to issue securities to the amount of $10,000 a mile which will have priority over the security that is given for the $45,000,000.
More than that.

Well, up to $25,000, but
those securities will have priority over and will not be subsequent to the $45,000,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman
will look at subsection 2 of section 2 of the resolution he will see that that point is covered.

That settles the point
that I had in mind, namely that if the Canadian Northern were limited in its issue of further securities by the mortgage now being given, they would be practically prohibited from issuing securities and there would be no means of raising the money that would enable these lines to be completed. But if they have already the prior right and that right is not interfered with, I presume that their position is not prejudiced. While it is quite proper to say that a benefit would naturally result to the residents along a branch line in the prairie provinces from the completion of the main line of the Canadian Northern either east or west or both, the advantage of the completion of the main line is slight as compared with the primary necessity of getting railroad communication at all. To the man who is in the woods 20 or 30 miles from a railroad, the railroad which will enable him to get to his market 'town is the first necessity; whether that railroad has connection with the Atlantic or with the Pacific is of secondary importance to him.
It is important to him to have at least one exit.

The Canadian Northern
have built up a system of some four or five thousand miles in the prairie provinces without a connection either east or west, and that four or five thousand miles has been of immense advantage to the business of the people and the settlemeet of the country. Thus the completion of the main iline, while we admit it is an advantage, is not of the same primary necessity that the( actual construction of branch lines, which have been guaranteed by the provinces, is to the people settled in that part of the country.

Of course, there is the consideration that preventing the road going into the hands of a receiver and Strengthening its position would strengthen also the position of branch lines connected with it, and would be more likely to conduce to their extension.

Undoubtedly unless such a condition were created as made the extension of branch lines impossible.
On section 10:
That in so far as the Canadian Northern and the constituent and subsidiary companies may be subject to the legislative Jurisdiction of the
Parliament of Canada, every such company shall have full power to do all and every of the things authorized by the Act based upon these resolutions, or provided for in the agreement, and shall have full power, and be bound to make, do and execute from time to time, all such acts, deeds, matters and things as may be necessary or expedient for carrying into effect the full intent and meaning of the Act based upon these resolutions and of the agreement, and the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada is hereby empowered to do what may be necessary on its part in the carrying out of the provisions of said agreement.

I would like to fully understand the effect of the words.
And be bound to make, do and execute from time to time, all such acts, deeds, matters and things.
How doe3 that declaration 'affect the authority of the provinces which have chartered railways which railway companies have been brought under the jurisdiction of" this Parliament by the declaration that they are for the general advantage of Canada?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The words are limited, of course, to the scope of the Act and of the agreement.

For instance, the Canadian Northern Railway Pacific has a very special agreement with the Government of that province. The nature of the agreement was considered essential by the Government of that province. The agreement delegated to the Government of the province of British Columbia a certain authority over the operations of that road within the province and denied authority to the Government of Canada to set aside the provincial authority. iDo I understand that this section is for the purpose of absolutely limiting the effect of that agreement? what is the effect of it in regard to that special agreement?

I would say it is no relation at all to that special agreement. The purpose of the clause was simply to give a general enabling power to the various companies comprised in and covered by the resolutions to do what the resolutions provide. The effect of declaring the Canadian Northern Pacific or any other company to be for the general advantage of Canada is defined by the British Nortn America Act, and further defined by section 6 of the Railway Act. The effect in a word is this: that in so far as the provisions of any special Act incorporating a provincial company conflict with the general Railway Act, the provisions of that special Act no



longer apply, but are superseded by the provisions of the General Railway Act of the province of British Columbia or any other province as the case may be. That is the effect of the declaration, but the effect of this clause does not in the least degree add to the control of the Parliament of Canada or to the effect of the Railway Act upon the provincial line. The only control we have is by virtue of the declaration. This clause gives no further control at all. There is nothing within the four corners of the resolution which is antagonistic or in any way conflicts with that agreement in British Columbia or with any other road, except such as are done away with by the mere declaration that the road is for the general advantage of Canada. I repeat that this clause in no way adds to the powers of the Dominion Parliament or to the operation of the Railway Act upon a provincial company further than is already done by the mere declaration.
My hon. friend speaks of enabling the provincial company to do thus and so, but this clause is compulsory. They are bound to do thus and so.
When they accept these resolutions they are bound to carry out the provisions. They are bound to do what these resolutions look forward to their doing.
That is leaving it gloriously indefinite.
No, it is made specific and definite. These resolutions say that each and every company on acceptance of these resolutions are bound to do thus and so.
They do not have the acceptance of them. They are legislated out of one position and into another.

We cannot legislate
them into it at all. They accept these resolutions, and when the Bill comes down that will be more clearly seen. Perhaps I should have given the wording of the Bill. Subclause a of clause 3 of these resolutions oreads:
The agreement a draft whereof is set forth in the third schedule hereto, hereinafter called the ' agreement ' shall he duly executed by the parties thereto and the Governor in Council is hereby authorized to execute the same.
In the Bill it reads this way:
The agreement a draft whereof Is set forth in the third schedule hereto, hereinafter called the

' agreement ' shall be executed by the parties thereto when duly authorized so to do by appropriate by-laws or resolutions passed by each of the companies parties thereto accepting the provisions of this Act, and the Governor in Council is hereby authorized to execute the same.
It has been thought wise to have each of the companies accept that. We do not legislate that they must accept it, but we say that before the guarantee is given they must specifically accept this Act, and by due authority of resolution sign the agreement.

Does the Solicitor General say that any of these local companies can do anything by way of accepting the agreement if that power has not been' granted in its charter. I understand the law to be that a local company, in fact any company, must keep within the powers of its charter, and that it cannot pass any resolution that would surpass the power that is given to it by the authority creating the company, so if those local companies had not within then acts of incorporation power to pass such resolutions as the solicitor General mentions, would the passing of resolutions which were beyond their jurisdiction have any effect merely because we say that they shall have that authority. I rather think we have no power to confer such authority upon these companies if it is not granted in their acts of incorporation.

It must be remembered that this Act is passed first, the resolutions come next, and the agreement is then signed. Immediately this Act is passed those companies become Dominion companies. They come under Dominion jurisdiction and our Railway Act, and I take it -I do not think it will be disputed-that any company under the Dominion Government has power to accept an Act passed in relation to it by the Dominion Parliament itself.

I quite understand
that, but I do not understand that we have power to lift out of their status as local companies half a dozen or so of small companies created by provincial jurisdiction, and bring them under Dominion jurisdiction without any act on their part and without the consent of the legislature creating them. I am not satisfied that we have power to create them Dominion corporations.
I think so.

I think that brings us to the question I discussed with the ri^ht hon. Premier before dinner as to the relationship between the Company and the provincial governments. There are provisions in these resolutions, on account of the wide powers that are given to the Governor in Council in connection with the drawing up of the trust deed, which may, and in all probability will, conflict with the provisions securing the stock guaranteed by the provincial governments. If I apprehend the meaning of these resolutions, it is something like this: Any of these companies that desires to take advantage of the provisions contained in the resolutions may accept those provisions preliminary to anything being done; and if an the terms of the new trust deed that is executed to secure the advances that are made, provisions are inserted which override and destroy the rights of the provincial governments under their deeds, then the federal terms will be supreme. That would seem to be the effect.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
So far as I am aware
there has never been any objection to the jurisdiction of Parliament over the whole system, except possibly during the period of construction of those roads in Alberta and Saskatchewan. Is that what my hon. friend is alluding to?
That is one of the things.

speechtext:
I do not see that there
would be any interference that would be prejudicial, for the reason that the provincial Government notwithstanding any legislation that we pass in this form would still 'have control over the expenditure of money. whether this general enabling and conditional clause does not give the federal Government power to include in these trust deeds provisions which will materially interfere with the securities of the provincial governments. All doubts could be set at rest by proposing to the appropriate clause, or inserting in the proper place, an amendment which would save the rights of the provincial governments in respect to these particular securities and afford such remedies as they would require.

The question is raised by my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) as to what would be the effect of this section. Under it the company are not only enabled, but compelled, to do certain things because there is power compelling them to do what is intended by this agreement. The answer of the Solicitor General was, and I think he was right, that we assume power over these companies by the fact that we declare them to be works for the general advantage of Canada. This brings me to the question raised by my hon. friend, from Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie). In my estimation all these roads which have been established by local charters come under the jurisdiction of this Parliament and we have control over them notwithstanding the fact that they were created by local charters. Section 92 of the British North America Act seems to make this point very clear. Section 92 declares what shall be under the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures. That section places under the control of the Dominion Parliament:
Such works as, although wholly situate within the province, are before or after their execution declared by the Parliament of Canada to be for the general advantage of Canada or for the advantage of two or more of the provinces.
These words seem to be very clear. The provincial legislature has control over works which are only situate in their province unless they are taken possession of by the Dominion Parliament by the declaration that they are works for the general advantage of Canada. Whether the works are constructed before or after the legislation is a matter of significance. If they are declared to be works for the general advantage of Canada before their execution, it is very clear that they are at once brought under the control of this Parliament; but if they have been executed under the provincial law, then, the moment they are declared to be for the general advan-

tage of Canada, the authority under which they are administered comes under the jurisdiction of this Parliament. By this resolution we take power over these companies and we take not only an enabling power, but a compelling power to compel them to do what we want them to do.
To the extent of complying with anything called for by this resolution.

To the extent of compelling the company to perform their contract even if it is not in accordance with their charter. This Parliament becomes supreme and this company can be compelled to do anything for the purpose of fulfilling this contract whether they will or not because they become subject to this Parliament. The provincial charter that has created the company is practically defunct now because the charter becomes a Dominion charter and we have power to amend that charter and to impose new conditions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The powers of the company remain as before until the Dominion Parliament proceeds to amend them. After the declaration the Dominion Parliament is the sole authority that has the right to amend them. Asi far as that is concerned provision is made that those companies may give a mortgage to secure the amounte of any moneys that may be expended on their respective roads out of the aid now provided. If they had no power before, the companies, under the appropriate sections, would have the power by reason of these resolutions and the Bill to be founded upon them. But that mortgage would not interfere in any way with any previous security created under provincial legislation. I cannot see that we would be interfering with such security by the proposed declaration.

Suppose there was a conflict about location, suppose the trust deed provided that the amount to be advanced would only be advanced upon the federal government approving of a certain location, and you have some other provision under the provincial trust deed, under this section the federal Government would be bound to control.

I think that is correct, but the provincial Government would be able to control the situation by reason of their control over the moneys to be expended upon the road. I would not apprehend the slightest danger of any friction in regard to that. If there be any danger the

provincial Government have control over the situation because they might decline to have their money expended unless the road was located in a particular place.

That is perfectly true. I do not suppose that this Government would oppose its will to the will of the local authorities in a matter of this kind but we have declared that these works are for the general advantage of Canada and having made that declaration this Parliament will determine what, according to its will, is proper to be done.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I appreciate what my
right Iron, friend says, but I would still be inclined to maintain that the provincial Government having control of these moneys, which are to be expended and are raised against provincial security, would have very ample control as far as location is concerned.
I am quite sure that under any power of this Parliament we will not take money from the provincial treasury.

We are declaring these works, under this resolution, to be for the general advantage of Canada and we are doing so, it seems to me, in direct violation, as far as one of these companies is concerned, of the legislation passed by the British Columbia Legislature in 1910. In that year there was an Act passed ratifying an agreement between the province of British Columbia, the Canadian Northern and the Canadian Northern Pacific Railway Company. In that agreement there is the following section:
The Northern Company agrees that the Pacific Company will agree that the Pacific Company shall not, and the Northern Company agrees that it will not, at any time apply to be declared a work for the general advantage of Canada.
One of the companies mentioned in that section of the British Columbia Act is the Canadian Northern Pacific railway which, by this resolution, is declared to be a work for the general advantage of Canada. Is not that declaration made in violation of the terms of this statute?

Not as I would read it. The statute binds the Canadian Northern Pacific not to apply to come under the jurisdiction of the Parliament of Canada. The Canadian Northern Pacific has not applied; but the Government under the circumstances feels that it cannot come to the assistance of the Canadian Northern Pacific,

in the way of doing it on its own motion, without declaring the Canadian Northern Pacific to be for the general advantage of Canada. There has certainly been no application.

There has been no application, but the Canadian Northern Pacific has been brought under the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners. As I stated on a previous occasion, there is an agreement with the province of British Columbia which takes the railway away from our jurisdiction. In fact there is an agreement somewhere in the resolution that all existing agreements shall he respected; and so far as the legislative authority is concerned, the Canadian Northern bound itself that at would not apply, and that it would not consent to the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners. Still, the moment we declare it a work for the general advantage of Canada, I think that it cannot avoid that jurisdiction.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
In so far as the position of the British Columbia -Government is concerned, it did -undertake to assist within the limits of that province a road which is necessarily part of a great transcontinental system. There was the agreement to which my hon. friend from Russell (Mr. Murphy) has alluded. We recognize that; it is on the face of the statutes, but it seems to me that the situation which presents itself to Parliament at the present time is this: If that road is to become, not only practically and naturally, hut legally a part of this great transcontinental system, the Board of Railway Commissioners	for Canada	must have
jurisdiction over it. Obviously the board must have jurisdiction over it in respect of through rates; and I think it would be most inconvenient and undesirable that the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada should - have jurisdiction over it in respect of through rates -and not in respect of local rates as well. Therefore as far as I am concerned, I would not feel disposed to come to Parliament and propose this guarantee, out of which a very large measure of aid must go to the Canadian Northern Pacific Railway Company, unless the Parliament of Canada were in the future to have control through its Board of Railway Commissioners over the rates on that road. That is the way I have felt about it, and I cannot see that any other policy is possible. It must be remembered after all that, when this aid is
voted for the Canadian Northern Pacific Railway Company, to ensure the completion of that road, the position of the company itself and the position of the province of British Columbia, as guarantor for a very large amount of that company s bonds, are 'materially strengthened. There can be no doubt about that. It is perfectly true that the agreement, to which my hon. friend the member for Russell has called 'attention, was made in connection with the guarantee of the company's bonds; but inasmuch as the situation of that company is strengthened and the position of the province of British Columbia is materially improved by the proposal to ensure the completion of that line, it does not seem to me that there was any other reasonable course to pursue than the one which we are now pursuing. We might have the alternative of proposing aid upon the condition that no portion thereof should be expended upon the line within the province of British Columbia until it has been declared a work for the general advantage of 'Canada. If we had brought down the aid in that way, I am sure that the province of British Columbia would have been very glad to consent. In fact, I think they would be very foolish not to consent in order to get the advantage of the aid. We propose to make that portion of the line part of this great transcontinental system. If there is any alternative that hon. gentlemen opposite can suggest. I shall be very glad to consider it. We do not for * one moment desire to interfere in this matter in such way as to prejudice contractual rights created between the province of British Columbia and the company; but we feel that, if we are now called upon to come to the aid of the road as a whole and seeing that a very considerable portion of that aid is to be applied to the line within the province of British Columbia, we have the right to insist and we do insist that that whole line from the Atlan-

Have any representations been made by the Government of British Columbia as to the ousting of their jurisdiction?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

Yes, they have made
representations to us and we have told them exactly what I have told my hon. friend from Russell. I shall be very glad

indeed to lay the correspondence upon the table of the House. I have told them, in so many words, that we do not feel disposed to guarantee the bonds and to bring this aid, a very considerable portion of which is to be devoted to the line within the province of British Columbia, unless the whole line from the Atlantic to the Pacific, including the line within the province of British Columbia, is made subject to the jursd'iction and control of the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada. That is the position which I am bound to maintain and which I intend to maintain; and it is a position which I think, in view of all I have said, in view of the whole situation, is a reasonable one, and one which in the end must work out, not only to the advantage of the railway company but to the marked advantage of the province of British Columbia itself as guarantor.

By this declaration, however, that the road is to 'be for the general advantage of Canada, I think that Sir Richard McBride must give way. I am not sure yet. We shall come to that later on. I have alluded to that on a former occasion.
I am not sure that the control is just as efficient as my hon. friend has stated, be-
cause there is somewhere in this resolution a provision to the effect that these agreements shall remain in force. When we came to that section, we may see how far it goes; but the intention to have the control of the rates everywhere must of course be paramount in this matter.

The section simply provides that, as respects the moneys and the trait deeds at guaranteed securities that are not under the present Canadian Northern railway, these moneys shall be secured by the individual eompanies on whose property they are expended by mortgages on their properties, assets, incomes and revenues payable to the trustee of the new trust deed as additional security. Sir'WILFRID LAURIER: I understand that, but the objection which at once arises in my mind has not been touched by my hon. friend. We become guarantors of a

loan of $45,000,000, and by section 3 we have taken a mortgage upon the undertaking of the Canadian Northern railway, its properties, revenues, etc., for every cent of that money. Now, any part of that money that is to go to the betterment of those companies is to create a special mortgage upon the assets of thoise companies. We have conceived the whole enterprise was one. If there is default in the securities, how are the proceeds to be divided? If we have one company and one only, one guarantee and one only, the proceeds of the moneys as they come from the treasury of the main company may be applied so much in Alberta, so much in Saskatchewan, so much in British Columbia, so much in Ontario, so much in Quebec. Upon this we take a special mortgage, in one place $1,000,000, in another place $500,000, in another place $3,000,000. I would have supposed that our mortgage would cover everything, not only the parent company, but the subsidiary company as well; that they should be all pooled, so to speak, and that no one portion of the money should go to one part and another portion to another part. Apparently it is proposed to proceed differently, and the reason has not been supplied by my hon. friend.

I think I have the objection which the right hon. gentleman raises; it is that we should have a mortgage for the whole amount, covering all the assets of all the companies. The first objection to that is that no company, no entity whatever, can possibly give such a mortgage. A company can give a mortgage only on its own assets; no company can give a mortgage on the assets of other companies. It could be done, of course, if amalgamation were possible; then the amalgamated company could mortgage all its physical assets. But amalgamation is impossible, for the reasons that I myself gave, supplemented by other reasons since given by other hon. gentlemen. So long as we keep the companies separate, all belonging, of course, to the parent company, but remaining separate entities in the meantime, as we are bound to do, so long we can only get a mortgage on the assets of those companies from the directors of those companies themselves. We will take the case of the Canadian Northern Ontario. . Suppose it received $15,000,000 as the proceeds of these moneys. It gives a mortgage for $15,000,000; does my right hon. friend argue that it should give a mortgage for $45,000,000? In

the first place, no object could be served. We have our $45,000,000 mortgage on the assets of the Canadian Northern, not only on the physical assets of the road but on the terminals and so on; we have it' on the stocks of the individual company and in that way the stocks of all the companies are pledged for the whole amount. But when we come below the stocks and down on the physical assets of the individual companies, we take a pledge in each case for the amount of money that went into those physical assets, which, I think, is the equitable .and fair thing to do. I do not think that our securities would be one whit better if we acted on the other principle and took a mortgage for $45,000,000 from each of the individual subsidiary companies, even though those companies get only a very small portion of the $45,000,000. It must be remembered that we have a mortgage on their stocks for the whole amount.

Does not the return

Mackenzie, Mann

000 of stock issued under authority of this Parliament. Mackenzie and Mann are the Canadian Northern, and in consideration of their transferring the stock in these subsidiary companies that they themselves hold to the Canadian Northern that they themselves hold, they are given $23,000,000 more stock of the Canadian Northern, while at the same time the Government is announcing to the country that it has reduced the stock of the company.

The hon. gentleman
knows that is not correct at all.

due deference, that it is absolutely correct; there is no question about it; the record says so. They have not done
that.

That is what they are
represented to be doing.

n:ch this Government is a two-fifths owner. That does not say Mackenzie and Mann own it still.

If the Government is to hold two-fifths and the company three-fifths, the total capitalization might just as well be $50,000,000 as

$100,000,000, and there would be that much less stock outstanding to earn dividends on the operation of the road. The Government has seen fit, without just cause or provocation, without sense of reason, to add $23,000,000 to the burden of stock issue against the Canadian Northern which will he a burden upon the earnings of the road in case of its ultimate prosperity. That is my point.

No there is not.
If the hon. gentleman will shut his eyes to that, all I can say is that none are so blind as those who will not see. There is to-day $145,000,000 of stock in all these companies.
In what companies?
In the subsidiary and parent companies.
Let us talk about either the subsidiary companies or the parent company; let us have them segregated, so to speak.

I will segregate them now. There is $68,000,000 of an issue against the subsidiary companies, there is $77,000,000 against the parent company; that makes $145,000,000 that now is entitled to dividends if any stock is entitled to dividends. When this Bill goes into effect there will not be $145,000,000 of stock entitled to dividends in any sense whatever, there will be $100,000,000, no more and no less. How can it be said that stock owned by the Canadian Northern is entitled to dividends and that the Canadian Northern stock too is entitled to dividends? Absurdity certainly could not go farther. The Canadian Northern stock, which represents the ownership by the Canadian Northern of the assets, may be entitled to dividends but nothing more can be. You have $145,000,000 entitled to dividends to-day; pass this Bill and you have $100,000,000 entitled to dividends. Is that a reduction or an increase?

You have $145,000,000 entitled to dividends to-day if any stock is entitled to dividends. Pass this Bill and
you have $100,000,000 entitled to dividends and $100,000,000 is $45,000,000 less than $145,000,000. Remember too that two-fifths of those dividends come back to the people of Canada, and remember too that the stock of Mackenzie, Mann and Company is reduced from $138,000,000 to $60,000,000. Yet hon. gentlemen will get up and say that we have increased the stock, and one hon. gentleman will say that we have doubled it. I presume that if we wiped it out altogether he would say that we had multiplied it a thousand times.

My hon. friend has not yet shown in all the arguments he has put forward where there is a word or a line in these resolutions that deprives this stock in the subsidiary companies of the right to obtain dividends.
The very result of the deal deprives it of that right.
My hon. friend says that is so but there is not a word in the resolution that says so.

My hon. friend must
agree that the stock cannot obtain dividends and the owners obtain dividends on the same stock. Imagine a railway company going to any sane tribunal and saying: We are capitalized for $100,000,000- but we own a lot of other stock and we want dividends on our capital stock and we want dividends on our own stock. The claim would be absurdity itself. It is the logical result of the arrangement that there can be only that $100,000,000 of stock that is being issued upon which they can claim to earn dividends.

My hon. friend has said
that and he has repeated and repeated and repeated it several times to-day.

For the reason that
otherwise it would be earning dividends twice.

But he not only does not put any form of words that carries that meaning in the; resolution but he declares that any such form of words as would convey that meaning cannot be embodied in the resolution. The subsidiary companies are subsidiary companies, they are individual entities, they are capable; of borrowing money and giving mortgages upon -their property. They have got to earn the interest on these mortgages, and by what process of reasoning does my hon. friend suppose that they are not entitled

to earn dividends on this stock just the same? It is true that the Canadian Northern will own that stock. If I owned it would that be a bar to their earning dividends upon it? Because the Canadian Northern owns the stock is that a bar to dividends being earned upon it? If the hon. gentleman wants to have it as be says it is, let him say so in the resolution. He believes it is that way now. He has been well instructed on that point but he has not made himself definite to the satisfaction of myself, or to the satisfaction of a number of other gentlemen in this House whose opinion on a legal matter is entitled to consideration.

Would the hon. gentleman suggest a clause to the effect that $100,000,000 would be entitled to earn dividends? We do not recognize that $100,000,000 as necessarily entitled to earn dividends but we say that no other stock shall be issued or shall have a claim to earn dividends. The company is not entitled to dividends. The\ owner of the stock may be entitled to dividends. The owner of the $100,000,000 of stock is the Canadian Northern Railway Company. If there was an amalgamation the Canadian Northern would be the owner of these roads. The roads would still exist. They will be worth just as much as if there was no amalgamation. Instead of the Canadian Northern owning them directly it owns them through this stock. How can you say that because it owns them through this stock instead of owning them directly it is entitled to an increased revenue?

How can my hon. friend
say that because the Canadian Northern owns the subsidiary companies through the stock of the subsidiary companies the stock does not exist?

I do not say that it
does not exist, but I say that you cannot count it twice in asking for dividends and you do count it twice when you say the Canadian Northern can ask for dividends on its own stock and also on the stock of the individual companies.
The subsidiary company is a separate entity and my hon. friend proposes to take a specific mortgage upon this separate entity.
It is a separate entity.

Powers are separately
granted to the subsidiary companies in order that they may pay the interest upon these mortgages; therefore the stock is entitled to earn dividends. The existence of the Canadian Northern Railway Company's stock has nothing to do with that because it does not affect the situation in any degree. On what principle is the Canadian Northern stock swollen by the handing over of $23,000,000 worth of it to Mackenzie, Mann and Company? My hon. friend has given half a dozen reasons. Amongst others he says Mackenzie, Mann and Company have given up a large amount of the claim that they have against the company, that they have rendered great services in the promotion of the company and that the Government is taking a part of the property of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. They do not do that at all. They do not put up the stock as security.

Well, my hon. friend and I cannot come to an agreement. As I understand the reading of the resolution, it makes certain and positive statements, and I believe I understand the English language as well as my hon. friend does. My hon. friend says there is a certain meaning and effect in these resolutions. I say that meaning is not contained in the resolutions, although it may be in his mind. I do not think we can come any closer together than that, if we argue here all night. Again I say, however, that he has no good and sufficient reason, no reason that will appeal to any man's sense of justice or fair play or public interest for the increase of the capital stock of the Canadian Northern by $23,000,000, and the handing of that $23,000,000 over to Mackenzie and Mann.

Thus my hon. friend, when he complains about all this water being turned in, in return for $23,000,000 worth of water in the Canadian Northern, has an absolute ground of complaint. Which stocks are water, in the opinion of the hon. gentleman?

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Macdonald) says he seeks information in vain. If he will only say what information he wants, I will make every endeavour to get it, if I cannot get it now. Has my hon. friend any authentic data as to how much actual money is represented in any of these items contained in the first Dart of the second schedule ?

I do not think we need rehearse the debate we have gone through, in this House two or three times. It is not money for the most part that is represented in these stocks. If a company undertakes the construction of a line of railway; constructs that railway, raises the money during construction, the parties who do are surely entitled at least to stock in the enterprise for their services. The courts of this country have held that they are entitled to remuneration for such services. They have performed the services; and I submit to the hon. member for Pictou, as a reasonable man:	Is
$10,000,000 worth of stock in an enterprise, in respect of which $35,000,000 or more *have been expended a reasonable amount of stock in return for services in financing and in the construction of that road? There is a case in the courts of Canada where it has been held that twelve and one-half per cent of the expenditure is a reasonable profit that could be sued for and recovered in cash. If accepted in the form of stock, it would naturally be more. In the face of that and in the face of the fact that the $1,000,000, in the case of the Halifax and Southwestern, represents the only return at all for the services of the contractors in the building of that road guaranteed them by the Government of Nova Scotia, it would hardly be said that they gave nothing at all for that million dollars' worth of stock. The same and similar explanations apply throughout.

There used to be an idea- of course, it has. been exploded long ago- that when people went into any constructive enterprise, they provided the money by way of stock. That idea seems to be discarded, and now apparently we do not expect any person to put up real money of his own. We start gigantic enterprises costing hundreds of millions of dollars, and we do not expect the enterprising gentlemen who start them to put up a dollar of their own money. It is nowadays expected that they make their money out of the enterprises instead of putting their money into them, as used to be the case in the old-fashioned days. Of course, the world moves, and we now are in a new age.
As to those stocks that are mentioned in the schedule and in regard to which the question arises how much is water, I noticed that the Canadian Northern Pacific is listed at $25,000,000. Now, the Canadian Northern Pacific, as I understand on the authority of the Premier of British Columbia, will cost $50,000,000. So, our enterprising friends are not taking 12J per cent of cost in stock, but 50 per cent of cost in stock. I do not know how much of that my hon. friend would consider to be water.
